clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Which famous landmark stands TALLER from ground to tip—Paris’s Eiffel Tower or New York’s Statue of Liberty?
clues.ahaFactoid: Iron lattice lifts the Eiffel Tower to 1,083 feet with its antenna, towering over Lady Liberty’s 305-foot pedestal and torch.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Which monument rises HIGHER into the sky—the Empire State Building or Egypt’s Great Pyramid of Giza?
clues.ahaFactoid: Even before its TV mast, Manhattan’s Art Deco icon hits 1,250 feet at the roof, nearly tripling the Great Pyramid’s 455-foot peak.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Which American suspension bridge boasts a LONGER main center span—the Golden Gate or the Brooklyn Bridge?
clues.ahaFactoid: Spanning 4,200 feet between towers over San Francisco’s strait, the Golden Gate stretches over twice the Brooklyn Bridge’s central span.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Which global city has hosted MORE Summer Olympic Games—London or Tokyo?
clues.ahaFactoid: London became the first three-time Summer Olympic host in 2012 after 1908 and 1948, edging out Tokyo’s two turns in 1964 and 2021.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Which US coastline touches MORE individual states—the Atlantic Ocean shore or the Pacific Ocean shore?
clues.ahaFactoid: Fourteen states from Maine to Florida meet the Atlantic Ocean, easily beating the five Pacific states along the western seaboard.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Which Olympic superstar captured MORE career gold medals—swimmer Michael Phelps or sprinter Usain Bolt?
clues.ahaFactoid: Phelps hauled in an unmatched 23 Olympic golds across four Games, while Jamaican sprint king Bolt claimed 8 golds across three Olympiads.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Which arena could pack in a BIGGER crowd—ancient Rome’s Colosseum or New York’s Madison Square Garden?
clues.ahaFactoid: Ancient engineers designed the Colosseum’s travertine tiers for roughly 50,000 spectators, more than double Madison Square Garden’s seats.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Which famous shipping canal stretches LONGER end to end—Egypt’s Suez Canal or Central America’s Panama Canal?
clues.ahaFactoid: Running 120 lock-free miles from Port Said to Suez, Egypt’s desert waterway is more than twice as long as Panama’s 51-mile crossing.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Which historic spaceflight completed MORE orbits around Earth—John Glenn’s Friendship 7 or Yuri Gagarin’s Vostok 1?
clues.ahaFactoid: Gagarin blazed the trail in April 1961 with a single 108-minute orbit, while Glenn circled Earth three times in February 1962.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Which famous corridor measures LONGER in total miles—China’s Great Wall network or America’s Route 66?
clues.ahaFactoid: Archaeological surveys tally over 13,170 miles of Great Wall sections across northern China, five times Route 66’s 2,448-mile ribbon.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Which Olympic Games welcomed MORE participating national delegations—Athens 1896 or Paris 2024?
clues.ahaFactoid: Just 14 nations sent athletes to Athens in 1896 for the modern revival, whereas 206 Olympic committees marched into Paris in 2024.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Which Cold War showdown lasted MORE calendar days—the Berlin Airlift or the Cuban Missile Crisis?
clues.ahaFactoid: Allied cargo planes flew food and coal into West Berlin for 11 months, whereas Kennedy and Khrushchev’s standoff resolved in 13 tense days.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Which monumental water drop stands TALLER—the concrete face of Hoover Dam or the plunge of Niagara Falls?
clues.ahaFactoid: Hoover Dam’s arch rises 726 feet above Black Canyon’s bedrock—over four times higher than Niagara’s famous 167-foot waterfall plunge.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Which named European conflict actually lasted LONGER—the Hundred Years’ War or the Thirty Years’ War?
clues.ahaFactoid: France and England fought on and off for 116 years, while the Thirty Years’ War lived right up to its round-number label from 1618 to 1648.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Which landmark book had a LARGER original print run—Shakespeare’s First Folio or the Gutenberg Bible?
clues.ahaFactoid: London printers struck roughly 750 copies of Shakespeare’s First Folio in 1623, well ahead of Gutenberg’s 180-copy movable-type Bible run.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Which founding American parchment carries MORE ink signatures—the Declaration of Independence or the US Constitution?
clues.ahaFactoid: Fifty-six delegates signed the Declaration of Independence, whereas thirty-nine delegates signed the US Constitution eleven years later.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Which NASA crew launched with MORE astronauts aboard—ill-fated Apollo 13 or Space Shuttle Columbia’s maiden flight?
clues.ahaFactoid: Lovell, Swigert, and Haise made a three-man crew on Apollo 13, while John Young and Robert Crippen flew Columbia’s maiden test as a pair.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Which US presidential sweep racked up MORE Electoral College votes—Ronald Reagan’s re-election or Richard Nixon’s?
clues.ahaFactoid: Reagan captured 49 states for an all-time record 525 electoral votes in 1984, narrowly topping Nixon’s 520-vote 1972 sweep.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Which storied rail journey covered MORE track miles—the Trans-Siberian Railway or the Paris-to-Istanbul Orient Express?
clues.ahaFactoid: Stretching 5,772 miles from Moscow to Vladivostok, Russia’s iron ribbon covers triple the distance of the classic 1,900-mile Orient Express.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Which postwar alliance started with MORE founding member states—the United Nations charter or original NATO?
clues.ahaFactoid: Fifty-one nations ratified the United Nations charter in 1945, whereas twelve Western nations signed the North Atlantic Treaty four years later.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Comparing just the metal figures without pedestals, which stood TALLER—the Statue of Liberty’s copper body or the Colossus of Rhodes?
clues.ahaFactoid: Bartholdi’s hammered copper Lady Liberty stands 151 feet from heel to torch, topping ancient accounts of the 108-foot sun god at Rhodes.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Which brutal World War II Eastern Front ordeal lasted MORE days—the Siege of Leningrad or the Battle of Stalingrad?
clues.ahaFactoid: German forces encircled Leningrad for 872 agonizing days from 1941 to 1944, more than four times Stalingrad’s 199-day urban struggle.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these Apollo flights actually landed astronauts on the Moon—which famous mission circled the Moon without touching down?
clues.ahaFactoid: Apollo 8’s Christmas Eve crew became the first humans to orbit the Moon in 1968, paving the way for Apollo 11’s landing seven months later.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these men appear on everyday US paper bills—which Founding Father has NEVER graced standard US paper currency?
clues.ahaFactoid: Washington ($1), Jefferson ($2), and Lincoln ($5) anchor our wallets, while second president John Adams never got his own circulating paper note.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these spacecraft series carried NASA astronauts—which spherical capsule launched Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin?
clues.ahaFactoid: Gagarin rode Vostok 1 into orbit in April 1961, ejecting at 23,000 feet to parachute down separately from his scorched sphere.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these countries formed the World War II Allied "Big Three" at Yalta—which nation fought on the Axis side instead?
clues.ahaFactoid: Churchill, Roosevelt, and Stalin met at Yalta in February 1945, while Japan remained aligned with the Axis powers until August.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these figures marched or led during the 1960s Civil Rights era—which leader belonged to the 19th-century Abolitionist movement?
clues.ahaFactoid: Orator Frederick Douglass escaped slavery in 1838 and advised Abraham Lincoln, a full century before Lewis and Hamer led Freedom Summer.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these tech household names launched in the 1990s—which music giant actually started way later in the 2000s?
clues.ahaFactoid: Amazon, eBay, and Google all debuted between 1994 and 1998, while Sweden’s Spotify didn’t launch its music stream until October 2008.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these monuments made the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World—which French Gothic cathedral rose over a millennium later?
clues.ahaFactoid: Builders laid Notre-Dame’s cornerstone in 1163 CE on the Île de la Cité, long after ancient Greek travelers drafted the original Seven Wonders.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these famous newspapers are British Fleet Street institutions—which daily flagship hails from Manhattan?
clues.ahaFactoid: Founded in 1889 by Dow Jones in Manhattan, The Wall Street Journal reports from New York, whereas the other three anchor British journalism.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these leaders served as British Prime Minister under Queen Elizabeth II—which wartime titan stepped down before her reign began?
clues.ahaFactoid: Chamberlain resigned in May 1940 and died later that year; Churchill returned as PM in 1951 to greet young Queen Elizabeth II in 1952.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these famous ships sank in headline disasters—which celebrated vessel still floats intact as a museum in Boston Harbor?
clues.ahaFactoid: "Old Ironsides," launched in 1797, remains the world’s oldest commissioned naval ship still afloat, resting proudly in Charlestown Navy Yard.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these legendary journalists anchored the nightly network news in the 1960s—which icon hosted late-night comedy instead?
clues.ahaFactoid: While Cronkite at CBS and Huntley-Brinkley at NBC delivered 1960s evening headlines, Johnny Carson ruled late-night talk on The Tonight Show.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these landmark summits took place during World War II—which 1995 peace accord brokered Bosnia’s settlement in Ohio?
clues.ahaFactoid: Negotiated at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in November 1995, the Dayton Accords ended more than three years of bitter war in Bosnia.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these Summer Olympics suffered huge Cold War boycotts—which peaceful post-Cold War Games had zero major nation boycotts?
clues.ahaFactoid: Montreal (1976), Moscow (1980), and Los Angeles (1984) each saw sweeping walkouts, whereas 1992 Barcelona united teams in full celebration.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these political scandals shook the 1970s or 1980s—which bribery scandal hit President Warren G. Harding back in the 1920s?
clues.ahaFactoid: Oil lease kickbacks in Wyoming’s Teapot Dome rocked 1922 Washington, half a century before Abscam and Iran-Contra.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these spacecraft suffered tragic loss of crew—which rugged mission brought all three astronauts home safely after an explosion?
clues.ahaFactoid: Through improvised CO2 scrubbers and a lunar slingshot, Mission Control brought Apollo 13’s crew safely back to the Pacific.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these real investigative newsrooms won Pulitzer Prizes—which fictional Metropolis paper employed Clark Kent?
clues.ahaFactoid: The Globe, Inquirer, and Herald boast shelves of real Pulitzers, whereas the Daily Planet exists only inside Superman’s comic panels.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these nations swept out Communist rule during 1989’s Autumn of Nations—which country did not dissolve into republics until 1991?
clues.ahaFactoid: East Germany, Czechoslovakia, and Romania transformed in late 1989, while the USSR lingered until December 1991.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these castles or palaces serve as British royal residences—which French chateau belonged to Sun King Louis XIV?
clues.ahaFactoid: Louis XIV turned a hunting lodge outside Paris into gilded Versailles, while British monarchs retreat to Windsor, Balmoral, and Sandringham.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these pioneering women served as elected heads of government in the 1960s or 1970s—which leader took office in the 2000s?
clues.ahaFactoid: Bandaranaike (1960), Gandhi (1966), and Meir (1969) shattered ceilings decades before Angela Merkel became German Chancellor in 2005.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these cities host major European Union institutions—which Swiss city hosts United Nations headquarters outside the EU?
clues.ahaFactoid: Switzerland has never joined the EU, making Geneva a UN and Red Cross hub while Brussels, Strasbourg, and Luxembourg anchor EU governance.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these legal landmarks hail from English constitutional history—which stone code was carved in ancient Babylon?
clues.ahaFactoid: King Hammurabi’s basalt stele predates England’s 1215 Runnymede Magna Carta by nearly three thousand years.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these nations mounted the secret 1956 invasion during the Suez Crisis—which superpower pressured all three to withdraw?
clues.ahaFactoid: President Eisenhower stunned Britain, France, and Israel by threatening financial sanctions unless they pulled out of Egypt’s canal zone.

clues.stem: Finish Martin Luther King Jr.’s unforgettable 1963 Lincoln Memorial refrain: "I have a [ _____ ] today."
clues.ahaFactoid: Gospel singer Mahalia Jackson shouted "Tell them about the dream, Martin!" mid-speech, prompting King to set aside his prepared notes.

clues.stem: Finish Abraham Lincoln’s opening line at Gettysburg: "Four score and seven [ _____ ] ago, our fathers brought forth on this continent a new nation."
clues.ahaFactoid: Lincoln’s entire 272-word Gettysburg Address took barely two minutes to deliver, leaving photographers scrambling before he sat down.

clues.stem: Finish Patrick Henry’s fiery 1775 Virginia speech cry: "Give me liberty, or give me [ _____ ]!"
clues.ahaFactoid: Biographer William Wirt published those famous words in 1817 based on eyewitness recollections from St. John’s Church in Richmond.

clues.stem: Finish the famous English translation of Julius Caesar’s brisk battlefield dispatch "Veni, vidi, vici": "I came, I saw, I [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Caesar sent the three-word Latin boast to the Roman Senate around 47 BCE after routing King Pharnaces II in a swift five-day campaign.

clues.stem: Finish Revolutionary spy Nathan Hale’s reported final words before his 1776 hanging: "I only regret that I have but one [ _____ ] to lose for my country."
clues.ahaFactoid: British officer John Montresor heard the young Yale graduate’s defiance and passed the account along under a flag of truce.

clues.stem: Finish Winston Churchill’s rallying 1940 House of Commons pledge: "We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall never [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Though millions remember hearing it live, Churchill actually delivered the speech to Parliament; an actor re-voiced it for radio later.

clues.stem: Finish John F. Kennedy’s 1961 inaugural pledge: "Let the word go forth from this time and place that the [ _____ ] has been passed to a new generation."
clues.ahaFactoid: Delivered in freezing 22-degree sunshine, Kennedy’s inaugural address lasted just 14 minutes and remains one of history’s most quoted.

clues.stem: Finish strategist James Carville’s blunt 1992 campaign war-room sign for Bill Clinton: "It’s the [ _____ ], stupid."
clues.ahaFactoid: Hanging in Little Rock’s war room between "Change vs. more of the same" and "Don’t forget health care," the middle line stole history.

clues.stem: Finish General Douglas MacArthur’s 1951 farewell to Congress, quoting an old barracks ballad: "Old soldiers never die; they just [ _____ ] away."
clues.ahaFactoid: President Truman had relieved MacArthur of command in Korea days earlier, yet 30 million Americans tuned in to watch his farewell.

clues.stem: Finish the classic Greek exclamation Archimedes supposedly shouted running from his bath after solving gold displacement: "[ _____ ]!"
clues.ahaFactoid: Meaning "I have found it," Archimedes’ cry later became California’s official state motto during the 1849 Gold Rush.

clues.stem: Finish General Douglas MacArthur’s 1944 radio broadcast wading onto Leyte beach: "People of the Philippines: I have [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Fulfilling his famous 1942 promise "I shall return," MacArthur actually repeated his iconic beach walk for newsreel cameras.

clues.stem: Finish Theodore Roosevelt’s favorite West African proverb on diplomacy: "Speak softly and carry a big [ _____ ]; you will go far."
clues.ahaFactoid: Roosevelt first wrote the line in a 1900 letter while Governor of New York, before making it his trademark presidential doctrine.

clues.stem: Finish CBS anchor Walter Cronkite’s reassuring nightly sign-off for nearly two decades: "And that’s the way it [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Cronkite retired the phrase on March 6, 1981, though he returned it for a special 1999 millennium broadcast.

clues.stem: Finish broadcast pioneer Edward R. Murrow’s signature closing words from wartime London and See It Now: "Good night, and good [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Murrow picked up the phrase from BBC radio announcers signing off during the Blitz, turning it into television’s gold standard.

clues.stem: Finish Franklin D. Roosevelt’s December 8, 1941 address to Congress: "Yesterday, December 7, a date which will live in [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: FDR crossed out "world history" in his typed draft with a pencil and wrote "infamy" by hand minutes before facing Congress.

clues.stem: Finish Margaret Thatcher’s punning 1980 party conference defiance: "You turn if you want to. The lady’s not for [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Speechwriter Ronald Millar cribbed the wordplay from Christopher Fry’s play "The Lady’s Not for Burning."

clues.stem: Finish the walnut sign sitting squarely on President Harry S. Truman’s Oval Office desk: "The [ _____ ] stops here."
clues.ahaFactoid: Made at a federal reformatory in Oklahoma, the poker-slang sign meant Truman refused to pass responsibility down the line.

clues.stem: Finish Benjamin Franklin’s gallows-humor warning at the 1776 signing: "We must all hang together, or most assuredly we shall all hang [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: John Hancock had just urged unanimity among delegates when Franklin broke the tension with his classic pun on British treason hangings.

clues.stem: Finish naval captain John Paul Jones’s reported retort from the battered Bonhomme Richard in 1779: "I have not yet begun to [ _____ ]!"
clues.ahaFactoid: Though his own ship eventually sank after the battle, Jones forced the larger British HMS Serapis to strike its colors.

clues.stem: Finish the rebellious Italian whisper "Eppur si muove" long attributed to Galileo after his 1633 trial: "And yet it [ _____ ]!"
clues.ahaFactoid: No contemporary transcript records Galileo muttering it before the Inquisition, though the motto later appeared on a 1640s painting.

clues.stem: Finish the explosive two-word French front-page headline Emile Zola wrote on his 1898 open letter defending Alfred Dreyfus: "[ _____ ]!"
clues.ahaFactoid: Newspaper editor Georges Clemenceau suggested the bold banner title, selling over 200,000 copies of L’Aurore in a single morning.

clues.stem: Finish Soviet Premier Nikita Khrushchev’s infamous 1956 Polish Embassy remark that rattled Cold War nerves: "History is on our side. We will [ _____ ] you!"
clues.ahaFactoid: Translators rendered the Russian idiom bluntly; Khrushchev later insisted he meant communism would outlive capitalism, not launch missiles.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Found by French soldiers in Egypt in 1799, my three stacked scripts gave Jean-François Champollion the key to ancient hieroglyphs!
clues.ahaFactoid: Carved in 196 BCE in hieroglyphs, Demotic, and Ancient Greek, I’ve rested in the British Museum since 1802.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Cast in London and rung in Philadelphia, I carry a famous jagged crack and a Leviticus verse about proclaiming freedom throughout the land.
clues.ahaFactoid: My final fatal crack widened in 1846 on George Washington’s birthday, silencing my clapper permanently.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Towering above Westminster beside the Thames, sightseers use my playful nickname for the 13.5-ton Great Bell inside Elizabeth Tower.
clues.ahaFactoid: Named either for towering commissioner Sir Benjamin Hall or prizefighter Ben Caunt, my booming E-natural chime started ringing in 1859.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? I’m not strictly one blue-and-white Boeing 747—I’m the radio call sign given to ANY US Air Force jet carrying the President.
clues.ahaFactoid: Air traffic controllers coined my call sign in 1953 after a commercial flight shared the same number as Eisenhower’s plane.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Linking Paris and Constantinople in plush wood-paneled dining cars from 1883, Agatha Christie set one of her grandest mysteries aboard me.
clues.ahaFactoid: Operated by Belgian company Wagons-Lits, my original route crossed the Alps and Balkans with lobster, champagne, and velvet sleepers.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Delayed by leaks in my companion Speedwell, I crossed the Atlantic alone in 66 autumn days to anchor off Cape Cod in 1620.
clues.ahaFactoid: Inside my cramped cargo hold, 41 male passengers drafted and signed a self-governing compact before stepping ashore.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Greeting arriving steamships past Lady Liberty from 1892 to 1954, my brick Great Hall processed over twelve million hopeful immigrants.
clues.ahaFactoid: Contrary to legend, inspectors didn’t carelessly invent new surnames—changes usually happened later at naturalization or by choice.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Built from short taps and long holds, my 1844 inaugural wire asked "What hath God wrought" between Washington and Baltimore.
clues.ahaFactoid: Inventor Samuel Morse was actually an accomplished portrait painter who turned to telegraphy after missing news of his wife’s illness.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Built with bicycle-shop spruce and muslin, I stayed aloft for just 12 seconds and 120 feet on a chilly North Carolina beach.
clues.ahaFactoid: Orville took the first historic hop on December 17, 1903, while Wilbur stretched the fourth flight of the day to 59 seconds.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Dragged from Welsh quarries and Wiltshire downs thousands of years ago, my towering stone lintels frame the midsummer sunrise.
clues.ahaFactoid: Builders raised my massive sarsen trilithons around 2500 BCE without iron tools, pulleys, or wheels.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Combining a screw wine-press frame with oil-based ink and cast metal letters in 1450s Mainz, I sparked Europe’s information explosion.
clues.ahaFactoid: My secret weapon wasn’t the press itself—it was a repeatable hand mold for casting uniform tin-lead-antimony letters fast.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Looking like a wooden typewriter with glowing lamps and scrambling rotors, Polish and British codebreakers cracked my wartime ciphers!
clues.ahaFactoid: Each keystroke spun my rotors like a car odometer, creating over 150 quintillion daily plugboard settings.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Unveiled on a 1947 magazine cover at seven minutes to midnight, atomic scientists nudge my hands closer to catastrophe or peace.
clues.ahaFactoid: Artist Martyl Langsdorf sketched me in bright orange and black for the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists’ first cover.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Hammered together at Promontory Summit, Utah, with a ceremonial Golden Spike in May 1869, I shrank a six-month wagon trek to one week.
clues.ahaFactoid: Both Leland Stanford and Thomas Durant famously swung and missed the silver hammer on the first try before a telegrapher tapped "DONE!"

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Buried 50 feet beneath Flushing Meadows at the 1939 New York World’s Fair, my Cupaloy torpedo shouldn’t be opened until the year 6939.
clues.ahaFactoid: I hold a Sears catalog, Einstein’s letter, a slide rule, and microfilm instructions on how to build a movie projector from scratch.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Surrounded by freezing San Francisco Bay currents, I held Al Capone and the "Birdman" until 1963—and starred in a 1962 raft escape mystery.
clues.ahaFactoid: Named "Isla de los Alcatraces" after pelicans in 1775, I closed as a federal pen partly because barging fresh water cost too much.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Nicknamed "Station X" in Buckinghamshire, my Victorian mansion and wooden huts housed Alan Turing, crosswords geniuses, and early Colossus computers.
clues.ahaFactoid: Roughly 75 percent of my 10,000 wartime staff were women—and every worker kept the secret for thirty years.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Originally dubbed "Shangri-La" by FDR in Maryland’s Catoctin Mountains, Ike renamed me for his grandson before Middle East peace talks made me famous.
clues.ahaFactoid: Nestled inside a heavily guarded wooded park, I hosted Churchill in 1943 and the historic 1978 Egypt-Israel accords.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Tucked inside tall clay jars in arid Qumran caves, a young Bedouin shepherd stumbled upon my 2,000-year-old Hebrew parchments in 1947.
clues.ahaFactoid: Preserved by desert dryness for two millennia, my fragments include the oldest known copies of nearly every Hebrew Bible book.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Gliding above 70,000 feet with bicycle-style landing gear and wide sailplane wings, Soviet missiles downed Francis Gary Powers while flying me.
clues.ahaFactoid: Designed at Lockheed’s Skunk Works in just eight months, pilots still fly upgraded versions of my tricky high-altitude airframe today.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Ordered by William the Conqueror in 1086 so he could tally every acre, mill, and pig in England, my parchment survey still rests in Kew!
clues.ahaFactoid: Subjects nicknamed my relentless tax census after the biblical Day of Judgment because no property owner could appeal its verdict.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Code-named by Ian Fleming’s naval intelligence circle in 1943, I floated fake officer "Major William Martin" ashore in Spain to fool Axis generals away from Sicily.
clues.ahaFactoid: Carrying theater stubs, love letters, and forged invasion plans in a chained briefcase, the hoax pulled German divisions away to Greece.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which landmark tech debut came FIRST—humans walking on the Moon or Apple’s original iPhone launch?
clues.ahaFactoid: Neil Armstrong stepped onto lunar dust in July 1969, nearly 38 years before Steve Jobs unveiled the first iPhone in January 2007.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which aviation milestone happened FIRST—the Wright brothers’ flight at Kitty Hawk or Charles Lindbergh crossing the Atlantic?
clues.ahaFactoid: In barely 24 years, aviation leaped from Orville Wright’s 1903 beach hop to Lindbergh’s 33-hour solo Atlantic crossing in 1927.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which global headline came FIRST—the end of World War II or the outbreak of the Korean War?
clues.ahaFactoid: World War II ended in September 1945 aboard USS Missouri, five years before North Korean troops crossed the 38th parallel in June 1950.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which American turning point struck FIRST—the Wall Street Stock Market Crash or the repeal of alcohol Prohibition?
clues.ahaFactoid: Black Tuesday hit Wall Street in October 1929; four weary years later, the 21st Amendment reopened legal taps in December 1933.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which Disney theme park opened its gates FIRST—Disneyland in Anaheim or Walt Disney World in Florida?
clues.ahaFactoid: Walt Disney welcomed guests to Anaheim in July 1955; Magic Kingdom near Orlando opened sixteen years later in October 1971.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which chart-shattering music smash hit FIRST—Elvis Presley’s "Heartbreak Hotel" or Michael Jackson’s "Thriller"?
clues.ahaFactoid: Elvis topped Billboard in early 1956 with "Heartbreak Hotel," twenty-six years before "Thriller" rewrote pop history in late 1982.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which US landmark law passed FIRST—the 19th Amendment granting women’s suffrage or the Civil Rights Act?
clues.ahaFactoid: Ratified in August 1920, women’s suffrage preceded Lyndon B. Johnson’s sweeping Civil Rights Act of July 1964 by 44 years.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which global sports tournament held its inaugural edition FIRST—the modern Olympic Games or the FIFA World Cup?
clues.ahaFactoid: Athens revived the Olympic Games in 1896, thirty-four years before Uruguay hosted and won the inaugural FIFA World Cup in 1930.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which dramatic Roman headline happened FIRST—Julius Caesar crossing the Rubicon or Mount Vesuvius burying Pompeii?
clues.ahaFactoid: Caesar’s famous "die is cast" river crossing occurred in 49 BCE—well over a century before Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which revolutionary spark flew FIRST—the US Declaration of Independence or the storming of the Bastille in Paris?
clues.ahaFactoid: Philadelphia delegates adopted independence in July 1776; Parisians stormed the Bastille fortress thirteen years later in July 1789.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which pop-culture phenomenon arrived FIRST—the original Star Wars movie or MTV’s first cable broadcast?
clues.ahaFactoid: Luke Skywalker blasted onto movie screens in May 1977; MTV debuted four years later in August 1981 playing "Video Killed the Radio Star."

clues.stem: Before or After? Which World War II turning point unfolded FIRST—the attack on Pearl Harbor or the Allied D-Day landings in Normandy?
clues.ahaFactoid: December 7, 1941 drew the United States into World War II, two and a half years before Allied forces stormed Normandy on June 6, 1944.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which orbital landmark blasted off FIRST—the Hubble Space Telescope or the first module of the International Space Station?
clues.ahaFactoid: Space Shuttle Discovery carried Hubble into orbit in April 1990; Russia launched the first ISS module Zarya eight years later in November 1998.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which modern milestone happened FIRST—Nelson Mandela’s inauguration as President or Euro paper cash entering wallets?
clues.ahaFactoid: Mandela took the presidential oath in Pretoria in May 1994, whereas physical Euro banknotes and coins arrived in January 2002.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which Cold War headline took place FIRST—the US-Soviet Apollo-Soyuz orbital handshake or the Chernobyl nuclear accident?
clues.ahaFactoid: Astronauts and cosmonauts shook hands in orbit in July 1975—nearly eleven years before Chernobyl’s reactor explosion in April 1986.

clues.stem: Before or After? Both joined the Union in the same year, yet which future star came FIRST on the US flag—Alaska or Hawaii?
clues.ahaFactoid: Alaska became the 49th US state in January 1959, beating 50th state Hawaii by seven months to earn a brief 49-star flag.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which communications breakthrough happened FIRST—the first transatlantic telegraph cable message or Alexander Graham Bell’s telephone patent?
clues.ahaFactoid: Queen Victoria and President Buchanan exchanged undersea telegraph greetings in August 1858—eighteen years before Bell’s 1876 patent.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which sweeping Asian headline occurred FIRST—India’s independence from Britain or the founding of the People’s Republic of China?
clues.ahaFactoid: Jawaharlal Nehru proclaimed India’s "tryst with destiny" in August 1947; Mao Zedong proclaimed the PRC in October 1949.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which Depression-era engineering marvel opened to the public FIRST—the Empire State Building or the Golden Gate Bridge?
clues.ahaFactoid: New York’s tallest tower opened May 1, 1931—six years ahead of San Francisco’s famed orange-vermilion suspension bridge in May 1937.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which legendary expedition triumph came FIRST—Roald Amundsen reaching the South Pole or Howard Carter opening Tutankhamun’s tomb?
clues.ahaFactoid: Norwegian explorer Amundsen planted his flag at the South Pole in December 1911; Carter glimpsed Tut’s "wonderful things" in November 1922.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which medieval milestone happened FIRST—King John sealing Magna Carta at Runnymede or Marco Polo setting out from Venice?
clues.ahaFactoid: English barons forced Magna Carta in June 1215, fifty-six years before young Marco Polo left Venice for Kublai Khan’s court in 1271.

clues.stem: Before or After? Just two years apart in the 1450s, which pivotal event came FIRST—Ottoman forces capturing Constantinople or Gutenberg finishing his Bible?
clues.ahaFactoid: Sultan Mehmed II entered Constantinople in May 1453, while Gutenberg’s first printed Bibles reached buyers around 1455.

clues.stem: Which famous North London street crossing did the Beatles stride across in single file for their iconic 1969 album cover?
clues.ahaFactoid: Photographer Iain Macmillan stood on a stepladder for just ten minutes while a bobby held traffic outside EMI’s St. John’s Wood studios.

clues.stem: In May 1953, New Zealander Edmund Hillary and Sherpa mountaineer Tenzing Norgay became the first confirmed climbers atop which summit?
clues.ahaFactoid: News of their triumph reached London just in time for Queen Elizabeth II’s coronation morning newspapers on June 2, 1953.

clues.stem: Which 25-year-old airmail pilot flew the Spirit of St. Louis nonstop from Long Island to Paris in 1927, becoming an overnight global idol?
clues.ahaFactoid: Nicknamed "Lucky Lindy," he carried four sandwiches, a canteen of water, and zero radio gear to save weight across 3,600 miles.

clues.stem: Which Atlanta Braves slugger electrified baseball in April 1974 by blasting home run 715 off Al Downing to pass Babe Ruth?
clues.ahaFactoid: Two college students sprinted onto the field to pat Aaron on the back as he rounded second, giving mother Estella the hug of the night at home.

clues.stem: Which 1975 Steven Spielberg shark thriller kept millions out of ocean surf and invented the modern summer blockbuster?
clues.ahaFactoid: Because "Bruce" the mechanical shark kept breaking down in saltwater, Spielberg hid him until Act Two—making the suspense twice as scary.

clues.stem: Which silent-film titan wore baggy trousers, a tight coat, a bamboo cane, and a bowler hat to create cinema’s immortal "Little Tramp"?
clues.ahaFactoid: Chaplin rummaged through Mack Sennett’s Keystone wardrobe room in 1914 and assembled the entire iconic costume in under five minutes.

clues.stem: Which virologist sparked nationwide church bells in 1955 with his polio vaccine—and declined to patent it, asking "Could you patent the sun?"
clues.ahaFactoid: Developed at the University of Pittsburgh with March of Dimes dimes from schoolchildren, Salk’s shot slashed US polio cases dramatically.

clues.stem: Which world-changing 1928 antibiotic did Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming spot when stray green mold wiped out bacteria on an unwashed dish?
clues.ahaFactoid: Fleming initially called his discovery "mold juice," and it took Oxford’s Florey and Chain a decade later to turn it into a wartime lifesaver.

clues.stem: A former textile worker and amateur skydiver, which Soviet cosmonaut became the first woman in outer space aboard Vostok 6 in June 1963?
clues.ahaFactoid: Flying under the call sign "Chaika" (Seagull), Tereshkova orbited Earth 48 times—more than all American Mercury astronauts combined.

clues.stem: Which pioneering 1964 British pirate radio station broadcast non-stop pop rock from an anchored ferry in international waters outside BBC reach?
clues.ahaFactoid: Founder Ronan O’Rahilly named the shipboard station after JFK’s daughter Caroline, helping kickstart Britain’s 1960s pop radio revolution.

clues.stem: New York Times Extra, April 16, 1912: "Giant Liner Sinks Four Hours After Hitting [ _____ ]; 866 Rescued by Carpathia."
clues.ahaFactoid: Because Marconi wireless signals were spotty overnight, early rival papers mistakenly printed that every Titanic passenger was safely towed.

clues.stem: Variety Box Office Flash, May 1977: "Record lines snake down Hollywood Boulevard as George Lucas’s space adventure [ _____ ] blasts off."
clues.ahaFactoid: Opening on just 32 screens nationwide, the film sold out so ferociously that Mann’s Chinese Theatre couldn’t empty aisles fast enough.

clues.stem: Cape Kennedy Wire, July 16, 1969: "Clock hits zero! We have a liftoff on the historic [ _____ ] Eleven voyage to the Moon."
clues.ahaFactoid: More than one million spectators jammed Florida’s beaches and causeways around Pad 39A to watch the Saturn V shake the earth.

clues.stem: London Gazette Special, June 2, 1953: "Rain pelts Westminster Abbey as millions gather around living-room TVs for Queen Elizabeth’s [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Twenty-seven million Britons watched on tiny monochrome sets, sparking Britain’s biggest wave of television purchases in history.

clues.stem: Times Square Ticker, August 14, 1945: "Confetti snowstorms bury Broadway as Japan accepts terms to end [ _____ ] War Two."
clues.ahaFactoid: President Truman announced Japan’s surrender at 7 p.m. Washington time, triggering spontaneous street dances from Times Square to San Francisco.

clues.stem: Manchester Evening News, July 25, 1978: "Healthy baby girl Louise Brown enters history in Oldham as the world’s first [ _____ ] baby."
clues.ahaFactoid: Pioneers Patrick Steptoe and Robert Edwards received a flood of joyous letters—and Edwards later won the 2010 Nobel Prize in Medicine.

clues.stem: San Francisco Chronicle Extra, October 17, 1989: "Game Three of the Bay Bridge World Series suspended as the [ _____ ] earthquake jolts California."
clues.ahaFactoid: Al Michaels was live on ABC pregame coverage when the studio lights shook, immediately turning sportscasters into breaking-news reporters.

clues.stem: Cambridge Science Bulletin, April 1953: "Watson and Crick publish a one-page Nature letter revealing DNA’s twisting double [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Rosalind Franklin’s razor-sharp X-ray diffraction "Photo 51" proved the crucial geometric key behind their molecular model.

clues.stem: Washington Post Banner, August 9, 1974: "Facing near-certain Senate conviction, Richard Nixon makes history with first presidential [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Nixon signed a crisp single-sentence letter to Secretary of State Henry Kissinger at 11:35 a.m., moments before Gerald Ford took the oath.

clues.stem: Cairo Dispatch, November 1922: "Howard Carter peers by candle flame into the glittering intact burial chamber of boy pharaoh [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: When patron Lord Carnarvon asked "Can you see anything?" Carter famously whispered back, "Yes, wonderful things!"

clues.stem: Picture This on 1968 Color TV: In Mexico City, two shoeless US sprinters bow their heads and raise black-gloved fists on the medal stand—name that pair.
clues.ahaFactoid: Silver medalist Peter Norman of Australia wore an Olympic Project for Human Rights badge beside Tommie Smith and John Carlos in quiet solidarity.

clues.stem: Picture This Street Scene, 1954: Marilyn Monroe laughs as a passing Manhattan subway train sends her ivory pleated dress swirling skyward—for which film?
clues.ahaFactoid: Thousands of onlookers whistled so loudly on Lexington Avenue that Billy Wilder had to reshoot the iconic moment quietly on a Hollywood soundstage.

clues.stem: Picture This 1994 Front Page: Joyful voters snake for miles under golden sun to cast South Africa’s first multiracial ballots—which historic party won?
clues.ahaFactoid: Winning 62.6 percent of the vote, the ANC inaugurated former political prisoner Nelson Mandela as president two weeks later.

clues.stem: Picture This 1969 Launch Pad: A 363-foot white-and-black Saturn V rocket roars clear of Pad 39A in sheets of orange fire—at which Florida spaceport?
clues.ahaFactoid: Pad 39A later launched Space Shuttle missions and commercial Falcon Heavy rockets from the exact same Merritt Island concrete flame trench.

clues.stem: Picture This 1957 Newsreel: Nine poised teenagers walk up school steps flanked by 101st Airborne paratroopers into Central High—in which Arkansas city?
clues.ahaFactoid: Elizabeth Eckford’s calm walk alone on the first morning became one of the defining photographs of American school integration.

clues.stem: Picture This 1970 Cold War Moment: On wet stone in Poland, West German Chancellor Willy Brandt drops silently to his knees—before which monument?
clues.ahaFactoid: Called the "Kniefall von Warschau," Brandt’s unscripted gesture stunned reporters and helped earn him the 1971 Nobel Peace Prize.

clues.stem: Picture This Sports Cover: Muhammad Ali stands snarling over a floored Sonny Liston in Lewiston, Maine—how fast into Round 1 did the phantom punch strike?
clues.ahaFactoid: Sports Illustrated photographer Neil Leifer snapped the overhead masterpiece from ringside as the fight ended at 2:12 of Round One.

clues.stem: Picture This 1947 Voyage: Six sunburned explorers steer a lashed balsa-wood raft flying a Peruvian-style sail 4,300 miles to Polynesia—name their vessel.
clues.ahaFactoid: Thor Heyerdahl built the raft using zero modern wire or nails, crashing safely onto Raroia atoll after 101 days at sea.

clues.stem: Picture This 1929 Aerial Shot: A sleek German airship glides low over Tokyo Bay during the first lighter-than-air circumnavigation—name Hugo Eckener’s ship.
clues.ahaFactoid: Financed partly by William Randolph Hearst, the Graf Zeppelin circled the globe in 21 days with journalist Lady Grace Drummond-Hay aboard.

clues.stem: Picture This 1966 Orbit Frame: Floating outside an open hatch with Earth’s blue horizon gleaming behind his gold visor, Buzz Aldrin snapped space’s first selfie on which mission?
clues.ahaFactoid: Unlike earlier grueling spacewalks, Aldrin used newly added handholds and underwater training to work smoothly outside for over two hours.

clues.stem: Spot the Myth! Three Revolutionary War facts check out—which famous midnight-ride detail is patriotic folklore, not history?
clues.ahaFactoid: Colonists still considered themselves British subjects in 1775, and secrecy mattered—Revere quietly warned "The Regulars are coming out!"

clues.stem: Spot the Myth! Three facts about George Washington are genuine history—which wholesome childhood story was invented after his death?
clues.ahaFactoid: Parson Mason Locke Weems invented the cherry tree yarn in his 1806 bestseller to teach young readers moral honesty.

clues.stem: Spot the Myth! Three French Revolution facts are true—which notorious royal quote was pinned on Marie Antoinette without proof?
clues.ahaFactoid: Jean-Jacques Rousseau wrote "let them eat brioche" about an unnamed princess when Marie Antoinette was still a child in Austria.

clues.stem: Spot the Myth! Three statements about 1492 navigation are true—which classroom cliché about Christopher Columbus is a 19th-century fable?
clues.ahaFactoid: Educated sailors knew Earth was round; Washington Irving’s 1828 biography popularized the myth that scholars mocked Columbus over a flat world.

clues.stem: Spot the Myth! Three facts about ancient Rome’s Great Fire of 64 CE are true—which famous image of Emperor Nero is completely impossible?
clues.ahaFactoid: Violins didn’t exist for another 1,400 years, and Roman historian Tacitus noted Nero was 35 miles away at Antium when the fire began.

clues.stem: Spot the Myth! Three facts about the 1929 Wall Street Crash check out—which lurid legend about ruined brokers was wildly overblown?
clues.ahaFactoid: Winston Churchill joked about fake jumper rumors in his hotel, yet New York suicide rates that autumn actually sat below summer averages.

clues.stem: Spot the Myth! Three Founding Father stories are authentic—which bird story about Benjamin Franklin misreads a private joke letter?
clues.ahaFactoid: Franklin never lobbied Congress for a turkey emblem; in a 1784 letter to his daughter he merely teased the bald eagle’s scavenging habits.

clues.stem: Spot the Myth! Three Revolutionary War flag stories hold up—which beloved Betsy Ross claim lacks any 1776 archival documentation?
clues.ahaFactoid: Ross was a real Philadelphia upholsterer who sewed ships’ pennants, yet her grandson first shared the George Washington parlor visit in 1870.

clues.stem: Spot the Myth! Three WWII British intelligence facts are verified—which dark rumor about Winston Churchill and Coventry was debunked?
clues.ahaFactoid: Declassified Ultra files proved Churchill learned an attack was coming, not which city—Coventry’s name arrived only hours after his car left London.

clues.stem: Spot the Myth! Three facts about ancient Alexandria’s Great Library are solid—which dramatic demise is historian myth?
clues.ahaFactoid: Caesar’s 48 BCE harbor blaze damaged dockside warehouses, yet scholars still worked in Alexandria centuries later through slow budget cuts.

clues.stem: 1960 Debate Check: During America’s first televised presidential clash, which audience thought Richard Nixon held the edge over JFK—radio listeners or TV viewers?
clues.ahaFactoid: Television viewers favored tanned, well-rested John F. Kennedy, while radio listeners who couldn’t see Nixon’s five-o’clock shadow leaned toward Nixon.

clues.stem: Copper Check: When the Statue of Liberty was unveiled in New York Harbor in 1886, what shade was her outer copper skin?
clues.ahaFactoid: Salty sea air oxidized Lady Liberty’s copper over roughly twenty years, turning her reddish-brown sheets into iconic verdigris green by 1906.

clues.stem: Festival Finale: At 1969’s Woodstock festival, when did Jimi Hendrix actually take the stage to play his electric "Star-Spangled Banner"?
clues.ahaFactoid: Rain delays pushed Hendrix back until around 8:30 a.m. Monday, when roughly 35,000 muddy stragglers remained out of 400,000.

clues.stem: Lake Placid 1980: When Team USA’s college hockey squad stunned the mighty Soviet Union, which tournament game was it—the medal-round opener or the final?
clues.ahaFactoid: Because 1980 used a four-team round-robin medal stage, Team USA still had to rally past Finland on Sunday morning to clinch gold.

clues.stem: Opening Day 1955: In which sun-baked city did Walt Disney carve his original Disneyland park out of 160 acres of orange groves?
clues.ahaFactoid: Opening day was broadcast live on ABC to 70 million viewers despite melting asphalt that trapped women’s high heels.

clues.stem: White House Tapes: During the Cuban Missile Crisis, what military measure did JFK announce on prime-time TV instead of an invasion?
clues.ahaFactoid: Attorney General Robert Kennedy and aides avoided the word "blockade" because under international law a blockade counts as an act of war.

clues.stem: Olympic Tape: How far was the very first modern Olympic marathon run from Marathon bridge to Athens in 1896?
clues.ahaFactoid: The extra 385 yards to hit 26.2 miles were added at London 1908 so the race could start at Windsor Castle and finish before the royal box.

clues.stem: Press Showdown: Which American newspaper broke the very first front-page installment of the leaked Pentagon Papers in June 1971?
clues.ahaFactoid: When a federal injunction paused the Times after three days, the Washington Post stepped up with its own copy from Daniel Ellsberg.

clues.stem: 1867 Treaty Desk: Which US Secretary of State signed the $7.2 million deal to buy Alaska from Russia—earning critics’ nickname "Seward’s Folly"?
clues.ahaFactoid: Coming out to roughly two cents an acre, the purchase looked far smarter once Klondike gold and Prudhoe Bay oil surfaced.

clues.stem: NASA Launch Log: Even though their names suggest otherwise, which twin Voyager spacecraft actually blasted off FIRST in August 1977?
clues.ahaFactoid: Voyager 2 lifted off August 20, 1977, sixteen days before Voyager 1—which rode a faster trajectory to overtake it past Jupiter.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Which Greek myth creature sports MORE heads—underworld guard dog Cerberus or winged horse Pegasus?
clues.ahaFactoid: Hesiod once gave Cerberus fifty heads, though nearly every classic myth depicts him as a fierce three-headed hound.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Counting Rudolph up front, which classic Christmas crew has MORE members—Santa’s sleigh team or Dickens’s Christmas Spirits?
clues.ahaFactoid: With Rudolph lighting the fog ahead of Dasher, Dancer, and the original eight, Santa pulls nine reindeer to Scrooge’s four ghosts.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? How does Scheherazade’s famous storytelling tally compare to the number of days in a standard calendar year?
clues.ahaFactoid: Scheherazade spun cliffhangers for One Thousand and One Nights—nearly three full calendar years—to save her life.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? In Greek myth, how does the number of thread-spinning Fates compare to the number of winged Furies?
clues.ahaFactoid: Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos spun mortal destiny as a trio—matching the three Furies, Alecto, Megaera, and Tisiphone.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? In medieval Camelot romances, which seating count was BIGGER—King Arthur’s Round Table or the Twelve Apostles?
clues.ahaFactoid: While later versions varied wildly, Thomas Malory’s Le Morte d’Arthur famously counted 150 seats around the Round Table.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? In classic nursery lore, which fairy-tale bird usually lays BIGGER golden eggs—Jack’s stolen hen or Aesop’s golden goose?
clues.ahaFactoid: Goose eggs weigh roughly twice as much as chicken eggs—though both stories prove greed ruins a magical flock.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Who peers through FEWER eyes in Homer’s Odyssey—giant blacksmith Polyphemus or hero Odysseus?
clues.ahaFactoid: Polyphemus had just one round eye dead center in his forehead, making Odysseus’s sharpened olive stake extra devastating.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Which winter holiday song or celebration spans MORE official nights—the Twelve Days of Christmas or the Festival of Lights?
clues.ahaFactoid: Running from December 25 to Epiphany on January 5, the Twelve Days of Christmas span four nights longer than Hanukkah’s eight.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Counting legs on mythic bodies, which creature walks on MORE feet—trickster spider Anansi or a Greek Centaur?
clues.ahaFactoid: West African folk hero Anansi scurries on eight spider legs, double a Centaur’s four horse hooves.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Which infamous mythic trio has MORE sisters—the Greek Gorgons including Medusa or Cinderella’s stepsisters?
clues.ahaFactoid: Medusa had two immortal Gorgon sisters, Stheno and Euryale, making three—outnumbering Cinderella’s famously mean pair.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? How many wishes does a classic fairy-tale lamp genie normally grant compared to the classic Three Little Pigs?
clues.ahaFactoid: Three rules folk magic everywhere—three wishes, three pigs, three billy goats, and three bear bowls of porridge.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? In Hans Christian Andersen’s "The Wild Swans," how many cursed brothers must Elisa rescue compared to Snow White’s dwarfs?
clues.ahaFactoid: Elisa weaves stinging-nettle shirts in total silence for eleven enchanted prince brothers—four more than Snow White’s cottage crew.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? In Greek myth, how many hands did each primordial Hecatoncheires giant swing compared to Briareus’s heads?
clues.ahaFactoid: Their very Greek name means "Hundred-Handed Ones," towering above even their own fifty roaring heads.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Which mythic group counts MORE goddesses—Apollo’s inspiring Muses or the fate-carving Norse Norns?
clues.ahaFactoid: Nine Muses governed epic poetry, music, history, and astronomy, tripling the three Norns—Urd, Verdandi, and Skuld—at Yggdrasil’s root.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? In Norse myth, which sacred tally is HIGHER—the days Yggdrasil’s eagle flies, or the wells feeding the World Tree’s roots?
clues.ahaFactoid: Three great roots of Yggdrasil stretch toward the Well of Urd, Mimir’s Well of Wisdom, and roaring Hvergelmir.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? At peak folkloric power, which mythical creature boasts MORE appendages—a full-grown East Asian Kitsune’s tails or Hydra’s initial heads?
clues.ahaFactoid: Ancient Japanese Kitsune and Korean Kumiho grow up to nine golden tails—matching the classic nine-headed Lernaean Hydra.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Counting scroll chapters, which Homeric Greek epic contains MORE books—the Iliad or the Odyssey?
clues.ahaFactoid: Alexandrian scholars neatly divided both the Iliad and the Odyssey into 24 books each—one for every letter of the Greek alphabet.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? In Arthurian and Irish legends, which royal court gathered MORE warriors—Fionn mac Cumhaill’s legendary Fianna or Arthur’s three-knight patrol?
clues.ahaFactoid: Led by Fionn mac Cumhaill, the Fianna rode across ancient Ireland in roving bands numbering hundreds of elite poet-warriors.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? In classic Maya cosmology, which cosmic realm stacked MORE vertical layers—the upper heavens or subterranean Xibalba?
clues.ahaFactoid: Maya priests mapped thirteen tiered heavens above the earth and nine shadowy underworld levels ruled by the Lords of Xibalba.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Comparing cyclic world ages in mythology, which tradition counts MORE grand eras—the Aztec Suns or the Hindu Yugas?
clues.ahaFactoid: Aztec myth places us in the Fifth Sun, Tonatiuh, whereas Hindu cosmology cycles through four great Yugas from Satya to Kali.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? In classical lore, which mythic bird lives LONGER before renewal—a traditional Greek Phoenix or a Persian Simurgh watching three world destructions?
clues.ahaFactoid: While Herodotus put the Phoenix’s cycle at 500 years, Persian lore says the wise Simurgh lived long enough to witness Earth remake itself thrice.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? According to the Prose Edda, how long does unbroken Fimbulwinter freeze Midgard before Ragnarok compared to the Trojan War?
clues.ahaFactoid: Fimbulwinter brings three straight winters with zero summer in between—terrible, yet shorter than Troy’s ten-year siege.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these Greek myth beings fly through the air—which bull-headed monster stayed trapped inside a Cretan maze?
clues.ahaFactoid: King Minos locked the Minotaur inside Daedalus’s winding Labyrinth until Athenian prince Theseus followed Ariadne’s thread.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these characters belong to Robin Hood’s Sherwood Forest gang—which cunning trickster came from Arthurian legend instead?
clues.ahaFactoid: Merlin advised King Arthur in Camelot, while Little John, Friar Tuck, and Maid Marian teamed up against the Sheriff of Nottingham.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these spooky staples trace back to Halloween traditions—which leaping reindeer leads Santa’s sleigh in December?
clues.ahaFactoid: Halloween blends ancient Celtic Samhain harvest customs with autumn games, while Dasher gallops strictly in winter Christmas lore.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these moral animal tales are classic Aesop fables—which wooden boy’s nose grew when he lied in an Italian novel?
clues.ahaFactoid: Carlo Collodi serialized Pinocchio in an 1881 Italian children’s magazine—over two millennia after Aesop’s Greek fables.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these iconic items belong to Norse thunder god Thor—which sandals belonged to Greek messenger Hermes?
clues.ahaFactoid: Thor rode a chariot pulled by Tanngrisnir and Tanngnjóstr while swinging Mjolnir; Hermes zipped across skies in winged sandals.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these magic props starred in classic fairy tales—which glowing light saber hails from modern sci-fi cinema?
clues.ahaFactoid: Cinderella’s slipper, Snow White’s apple, and Jack’s beans go back centuries, whereas George Lucas sparked lightsabers in 1977.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these creatures haunt lakes, forests, or mountains—which desert serpent legend belongs to Mongolia’s arid Gobi?
clues.ahaFactoid: Local herders dubbed the Gobi legend "olgoi-khorkhoi," contrasting sharply with chilly mountain Yeti and deep-loch Nessie.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these deities belong to the Roman pantheon—which goddess of wisdom kept her Hellenic name instead of Minerva?
clues.ahaFactoid: Athena was patron of Athens under her Greek name, while Rome worshipped her counterpart as Minerva alongside Mars, Venus, and Neptune.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these figures bring winter gifts or judge naughty kids in European lore—which playful cobbler hides gold at rainbow ends?
clues.ahaFactoid: Sinterklaas, La Befana, and horned Krampus visit every December, while Ireland’s cobblers-of-the-wee-folk guard pots of gold year-round.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these perils threatened Odysseus on his voyage home from Troy—which three-headed dog guarded Hades for Heracles instead?
clues.ahaFactoid: Odysseus braved Circe, Scylla, and Charybdis on the sea, though he only spoke to ghosts at the edge of Hades without fighting Cerberus.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these figures are American folk-tale workers—which fictional detective smoked a pipe at 221B Baker Street?
clues.ahaFactoid: John Henry, Pecos Bill, and railroad engineer Casey Jones grew into American folk ballads, while Arthur Conan Doyle crafted Holmes in London.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these Egyptian gods wear animal heads in temple art—which underworld ruler normally appears in human mummy wrappings?
clues.ahaFactoid: While Anubis, Horus, and Thoth bear wild heads, Osiris appears with green or black skin wrapped like a pharaoh’s mummy.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these spirits stem from Celtic and Irish folklore—which mischievous wood-imp hails from Central European Black Forest tales?
clues.ahaFactoid: Kobolds gave their name to the blue metal cobalt when German miners blamed sprites for toxic ore, unlike Celtic Pookas and Kelpies.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these places belong to Norse Nine Worlds cosmology—which sunny meadow of blessed heroes comes from Greek myth?
clues.ahaFactoid: Greek heroes rested forever in Elysium, whereas Norse fallen warriors banqueted in Valhalla inside gleaming Asgard.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these stories appear in classic One Thousand and One Nights editions—which wooden boy sailed inside a giant dogfish instead?
clues.ahaFactoid: Sinbad, Ali Baba, and the clockwork Ebony Horse thrill One Thousand and One Nights, while Collodi’s puppet swims out of Tuscany.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these figures appear in traditional Japanese folklore—which cunning prairie canine roams Native American Southwest stories?
clues.ahaFactoid: Shapeshifting Tanuki, cucumber-loving Kappa, and long-nosed Tengu fill Japanese scroll paintings, while Coyote stars in North America.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these Greek Muses inspired poetry, history, or astronomy—which winged figure was actually the dawn goddess Eos’s Roman cousin?
clues.ahaFactoid: Clio, Urania, and Calliope sang among the nine Muses, while Aurora painted rosy morning skies ahead of the sun chariot.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these knights rode for King Arthur’s Round Table—which Frankish hero blew his oliphant horn for Charlemagne at Roncevaux?
clues.ahaFactoid: Roland belongs to French "Matter of France" Charlemagne epics, whereas Gawain, Lancelot, and Percival ride for Camelot.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these characters hail from ancient Mesopotamian epics—which fierce storm-bird appears in Hindu Ramayana texts?
clues.ahaFactoid: Garuda carries Vishnu across Hindu epics, while Gilgamesh, Enkidu, and Cedar Forest guardian Humbaba march through Babylonian clay tablets.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these supernatural figures stride through Slavic folklore—which frosty Norse king ruled Jotunheim in sagas?
clues.ahaFactoid: Baba Yaga’s chicken-legged hut, the glowing Firebird, and woodland Leshy haunt Slavic lore, while Thrym stole Thor’s hammer up north.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these kami deities star in Japan’s Shinto Kojiki creation myths—which fiery spirit rules hearth fires in ancient Sanskrit hymns?
clues.ahaFactoid: Born from Izanagi’s ritual cleansing, Amaterasu, Susanoo, and Tsukuyomi anchor Shinto myth, while Agni blazes through India’s Rigveda.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these figures belong to the medieval Welsh Mabinogion—which legendary craftsman forged magic mills in Finnish Kalevala runes?
clues.ahaFactoid: Ilmarinen forged the mysterious Sampo mill in Finland’s Kalevala, while Pwyll, Rhiannon, and Bran headline Wales’s Mabinogion.

clues.stem: Finish the hungry giant’s booming rhyme from Jack and the Beanstalk: "I smell the blood of an [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Shakespeare actually slipped a close version of the "Fie, foh, and fum" giant rhyme into King Lear three centuries before modern printings.

clues.stem: Finish Goldilocks’s complaint after tasting Papa Bear’s big bowl: "This porridge is too [ _____ ]!"
clues.ahaFactoid: Robert Southey’s 1837 printed version originally starred a rude old silver-haired woman—Goldilocks only turned young and golden later.

clues.stem: Finish the Fairy Godmother’s magical coach makeover in Cinderella: she taps a plump garden [ _____ ] and turns it into a golden carriage.
clues.ahaFactoid: Charles Perrault’s 1697 French telling popularized the pumpkin coach, the lizard footmen, and the fragile glass slipper.

clues.stem: Finish Grandmother’s disguised reply when Red Riding Hood gasps about her big eyes: "All the better to [ _____ ] you with, my dear."
clues.ahaFactoid: Perrault ended his 1697 tale darkly with the wolf eating Red Riding Hood; the Brothers Grimm later added the rescuing woodsman.

clues.stem: Finish the joyful spring twist in Hans Christian Andersen’s classic tale: the teased Ugly Duckling grows up into a graceful [ _____ ].
clues.ahaFactoid: Andersen wrote the 1843 story partly as a heartfelt autobiography after feeling gawky and out of place in Copenhagen’s elite.

clues.stem: Finish the blunt truth shouted by a child watching the Emperor’s parade: "He hasn’t got [ _____ ] on!"
clues.ahaFactoid: Andersen adapted the vanity fable from a 14th-century Spanish storybook by Don Juan Manuel about invisible royal cloth.

clues.stem: Finish the hopeful wedding-and-luck superstition: "Find a four-leaf [ _____ ], and good fortune follows."
clues.ahaFactoid: Botanists estimate roughly one clover in five thousand grows a fourth leaflet—rare enough to feel magical in a grassy meadow.

clues.stem: Finish the age-old folk proverb about like-minded friends: "Birds of a feather [ _____ ] together."
clues.ahaFactoid: English writers were already repeating this feathered saying in the 1540s—even Plato noted a similar Greek proverb.

clues.stem: Finish the classic cautionary proverb—whose original Elizabethan form actually said "care"—warning nosy meddlers: "Curiosity killed the [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Playwright Ben Jonson wrote "care’ll kill a cat" in 1598, meaning worry, before 19th-century editors swapped in curiosity.

clues.stem: Finish the Aesop-inspired barnyard warning against premature bragging: "Don’t count your chickens before they [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: In Aesop’s "The Milkmaid and Her Pail," daydreaming about eggs and silk dresses ends with one clumsy toss of the head.

clues.stem: Finish the classic schoolyard fortune rule about a stray coin on the sidewalk: "Heads up, good luck; tails up, leave it [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: In folk custom, flipping a tails-up penny for the next passerby turns bad luck back into a tiny streetwise blessing.

clues.stem: Finish the spinning imp’s riddle song around his forest campfire: "Today I bake, tomorrow I brew; the next I’ll have the young queen’s [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: A sneaky royal messenger overheard the imp chanting his own name, breaking the baby-stealing bargain at the last moment.

clues.stem: Finish the famous Latin inscription promised on King Arthur’s Avalon gravestone in Thomas Malory’s telling: "The Once and [ _____ ] King."
clues.ahaFactoid: T.H. White later borrowed those four words as the title of his beloved 1958 Camelot tetralogy.

clues.stem: Finish the point-of-no-return Roman proverb linked to Julius Caesar’s shallow river march: "The die is [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Historian Suetonius wrote Caesar actually quoted a Greek comedy poet—Menander’s "Let the die be tossed high!"

clues.stem: Finish Daedalus’s desperate flight warning to his thrilled son Icarus before leaping off Crete: "Don’t fly too close to the [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Too low meant sea spray would soak the feathers; too high meant solar heat would melt the beeswax holding them fast.

clues.stem: Finish the thrifty tailor’s proverb urging quick small repairs before disaster spreads: "A stitch in time saves [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: First recorded in Thomas Fuller’s 1732 proverb book, the line pairs crisp rhyme with practical seamstress wisdom.

clues.stem: Finish Oedipus’s clever answer to the Sphinx’s riddle—"What walks on four legs at dawn, two at noon, and three at dusk?": "[ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Crawling as a baby, striding upright in adulthood, and leaning on a cane in old age solved the riddle and doomed the Sphinx.

clues.stem: Finish the classic fable punchline when an elderly mouse asks the cheering council: "Who will [ _____ ] the cat?"
clues.ahaFactoid: Still cited in boardrooms today, the fable mocks grand plans that ignore who actually has to take the dangerous first step.

clues.stem: Finish the beloved Scottish New Year’s folk song and friendship toast popularized by poet Robert Burns: "For auld lang [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Translating roughly to "for old long since," the Scots phrase became midnight’s global anthem thanks to Guy Lombardo’s radio broadcasts.

clues.stem: Finish the tragic Trojan curse Apollo laid upon princess Cassandra: she would always speak true prophecy, yet never be [ _____ ].
clues.ahaFactoid: She warned Troy not to roll in the Wooden Horse, only to watch citizens dance past her right into ruin.

clues.stem: Finish Homer’s favorite recurring poetic sunrise line across both the Iliad and Odyssey: "When young [ _____ ]-fingered Dawn appeared."
clues.ahaFactoid: Oral poets used "rhododaktylos Eos" as a handy metrical building block while singing thousands of hexameter verses by memory.

clues.stem: Finish stanza 77 of the Norse Poetic Edda’s Havamal: "Cattle die, kinsmen die, you yourself must die; one thing never dies—the [ _____ ] of a dead man."
clues.ahaFactoid: Old Norse "ordstirr" means word-glory—the living memory spoken around fires long after a warrior’s bones turn to dust.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Born when Perseus slew Medusa, I’m the snow-white winged stallion who carried hero Bellerophon into battle against the Chimera.
clues.ahaFactoid: Stamping my hoof on Mount Helicon, I even created Hippocrene, the sacred spring that inspired Greek poets.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? In Scottish farmhouse lore, I quietly sweep hearths and churn butter overnight for a bowl of cream—just never gift me clothes or I’ll vanish!
clues.ahaFactoid: Helpful household sprites like me only wanted porridge or milk; offering coats or trousers was taken as an insult—or freedom to leave.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Gifted by the Lady of the Lake and tossed back into glassy waters at Camlann’s end, a mysterious arm rose up to catch my gleaming blade.
clues.ahaFactoid: Geoffrey of Monmouth first Latinized my Welsh name "Caledfwlch" as Caliburnus, meaning hard-cleaver.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Clever trickster of Southern African-American folklore, I outsmarted Brer Fox by begging him NOT to toss me into the thorny briar patch!
clues.ahaFactoid: Born and bred right in the briar patch, my reverse-psychology escape stands as one of folklore’s sharpest turns of wit.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Gripping the whistle cord aboard Illinois Central Cannonball Express No. 382 in 1900, I stayed at my brake lever to save every passenger!
clues.ahaFactoid: Engine wiper Wallace Saunders wrote my famous railroad ballad shortly after that foggy April crash in Vaughan, Mississippi.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Gifted by a Cretan princess to Athenian hero Theseus, unspooling me along pitch-black maze corridors guided him safely back to daylight.
clues.ahaFactoid: Computer programmers still honor my name with "Ariadne’s thread"—step-by-step backtracking through impossible mazes.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Invulnerable to bronze spears and iron arrows, Heracles had to wrestle me bare-handed in a cave and wear my golden pelt forever after.
clues.ahaFactoid: Nothing could pierce my hide except my own razor claws, which Heracles used to skin my cloak for his First Labor.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Marrying King Shahryar to save my sister and myself, I paused every thrilling tale at dawn—spinning cliffhangers for 1,001 nights!
clues.ahaFactoid: By weaving stories inside stories across nearly three years, my voice won both mercy and literary immortality.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Gracing Wyoming postcards since the 1930s, my playful American campfire tall tale crosses a speedy prairie jackrabbit with pronghorn antlers!
clues.ahaFactoid: Taxidermist brothers Douglas and Ralph Herrick sparked my craze in Douglas, Wyoming, after mounting antlers onto a jackrabbit.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Tucked into pockets by American blues singers and carnivalgoers alike, folklore insists I bring the luckiest charm only if I come from the left hind leg.
clues.ahaFactoid: Linked to African-American Hoodoo folk magic and ancient European hare lore, I spawned millions of dyed keychain charms.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Sailors off Norway swore my sprawling tentacles looked like a rising rocky island before I dragged whole tall ships beneath icy waves.
clues.ahaFactoid: Marine biologists trace my terrifying Scandinavian reputation to rare glimpses of real 40-foot giant squid surfacing at night.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Unlike my wild carousing cousins, I was a wise Greek centaur healer who tutored young Achilles, Jason, and Heracles in Mount Pelion caves.
clues.ahaFactoid: Immortal and deeply learned in herbs and music, Zeus placed me among the stars as the constellation Centaurus.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Floating down a Japanese stream inside a giant peach, I grew up to recruit a dog, a monkey, and a pheasant to raid Demon Island!
clues.ahaFactoid: Bribing my animal allies with tasty millet dumplings (kibi dango), I returned home with the Oni’s stolen treasure.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Punished in Tartarus for cheating Death twice, I strain endlessly to shove a colossal marble boulder up a steep hill only to watch it roll back down.
clues.ahaFactoid: Philosopher Albert Camus famously turned my exhausting loop into a modern badge of grit, writing we must imagine me happy.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Connecting Asgard’s halls down to icy Niflheim, a dragon gnaws my deepest roots while an eagle perches atop my evergreen branches.
clues.ahaFactoid: Squirrel Ratatoskr dashes endlessly up and down my massive trunk carrying snarky insults between the eagle and the serpent.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Glowing across the sky in shimmering fire-red, watchman Heimdall guards my rainbow arch linking Midgard’s mortal earth to Asgard’s halls.
clues.ahaFactoid: Even Thor avoids stepping on me lightly—only crashing thunder and breaking my fiery arc signals Ragnarok’s final battle.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Sighted with glowing crimson eyes and wide silent wings near an abandoned West Virginia munitions plant in 1966, my town still throws a festival for me.
clues.ahaFactoid: Point Pleasant erected a gleaming twelve-foot stainless-steel statue of me downtown with shiny chrome abs.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Standing chin-deep under ripe fig branches, water shrinks and fruit whips upward whenever I reach—giving English a teasing verb.
clues.ahaFactoid: Yes, the word "tantalize" comes straight from my Greek eternal punishment after serving the gods a forbidden banquet.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Towering big enough in Sinbad’s voyages to lift full-grown elephants skyward, stranded sailors mistook my colossal white egg for a temple dome!
clues.ahaFactoid: Marco Polo even reported Madagascar tales of my giant feathers, likely sparked by fossil eggs of Madagascar’s extinct elephant bird.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Tossed into Midgard’s ocean by Odin as a tiny snake, I grew so colossal I encircled the whole earth biting my own scaly tail until Ragnarok!
clues.ahaFactoid: Thor once hooked me from a fishing boat using an ox head as bait—before terrified giant Hymir chopped the line!

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Slipping off my sleek ocean pelt to dance upon moonlit Orkney rocks, if a lonely fisher hides my sealskin in his chest, I must live on land until I find it.
clues.ahaFactoid: Gentle and heartbreaking compared to man-eating sirens, I swim straight back to sea the instant my hidden pelt returns.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Breathing flame across ancient Lycia with a lion’s forequarters, a bleating goat’s torso, and a hissing serpent tail, Bellerophon choked me with molten lead.
clues.ahaFactoid: Biologists still borrow my name today for any single organism carrying two genetically distinct sets of cells.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which classic storybook trickster debuted in print FIRST—Carlo Collodi’s Pinocchio or J.M. Barrie’s Peter Pan?
clues.ahaFactoid: Pinocchio’s wooden misadventures began serializing in Italy in 1881, over twenty years before Peter Pan flew onto London’s stage in 1904.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which legendary European fairy-tale collection hit bookshelves FIRST—the Brothers Grimm or Hans Christian Andersen?
clues.ahaFactoid: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm published Children’s and Household Tales in December 1812; Andersen’s first fairy-tale pamphlet arrived in 1835.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which beloved holiday classic appeared FIRST—the poem "A Visit from St. Nicholas" or Dickens’s "A Christmas Carol"?
clues.ahaFactoid: Troy, New York’s Sentinel printed "Twas the night before Christmas" in December 1823—twenty years before Scrooge met Marley’s ghost in 1843.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which iconic children’s fantasy novel arrived FIRST—L. Frank Baum’s "The Wonderful Wizard of Oz" or A.A. Milne’s "Winnie-the-Pooh"?
clues.ahaFactoid: Dorothy skipped down the Yellow Brick Road in 1900, twenty-six years before Pooh Bear hunted honey in Hundred Acre Wood.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which classic storybook came FIRST—Lewis Carroll’s "Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland" or Rudyard Kipling’s "The Jungle Book"?
clues.ahaFactoid: Alice tumbled down the rabbit hole in 1865—nearly three decades before Mowgli and Baloo roamed Kipling’s 1894 pages.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which famous British legend appeared in surviving written chronicles FIRST—King Arthur or outlaw Robin Hood?
clues.ahaFactoid: Welsh and Latin histories wrote about Arthur by the 800s and 1130s, whereas Robin Hood doesn’t surface in verse until the late 1300s.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which Disney animated fairy-tale feature arrived in theaters FIRST—"Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs" or "Cinderella"?
clues.ahaFactoid: Snow White charmed moviegoers in December 1937 as Disney’s very first full-length animated feature; Cinderella danced onto screens in 1950.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which American holiday tradition started FIRST in print—Groundhog Day in Punxsutawney or the phrase "trick or treat"?
clues.ahaFactoid: Pennsylvania’s Punxsutawney Spirit announced its first Groundhog Day trek in 1887; "trick or treat" didn’t appear in Canadian papers until 1927.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which real-life American folk legend lived FIRST—frontiersman Davy Crockett or heroic Illinois Central engineer Casey Jones?
clues.ahaFactoid: Born in Tennessee in 1786, Crockett fought at the Alamo over six decades before Casey Jones’s famous 1900 train wreck.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which mythic superhero leaped into comic books FIRST—Amazonian princess Wonder Woman or Marvel’s Norse Thor?
clues.ahaFactoid: Wonder Woman debuted in All Star Comics in 1941, beating Stan Lee and Jack Kirby’s Mjolnir-swinging Thor from 1962 by two decades.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which modern cryptid name hit headlines FIRST—Pacific Northwest "Bigfoot" or Puerto Rico’s "El Chupacabra"?
clues.ahaFactoid: Humboldt County newspapers coined "Bigfoot" around Jerry Crew’s giant plaster footprints in 1958, whereas Chupacabra sightings erupted in 1995.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which fantastical traveler book sailed into bookstores FIRST—Jonathan Swift’s "Gulliver’s Travels" or Baron Munchausen’s tall tales?
clues.ahaFactoid: Gulliver met tiny Lilliputians in 1726, nearly sixty years before Rudolf Erich Raspe published Munchausen’s outrageous moon flights in 1785.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which famous fairy-tale book came FIRST—Charles Perrault’s "Tales of Mother Goose" or Jeanne-Marie Leprince de Beaumont’s "Beauty and the Beast"?
clues.ahaFactoid: Perrault published Sleeping Beauty and Little Red Riding Hood in 1697—sixty years before Beaumont distilled Beauty and the Beast in 1756.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which gothic monster novel terrified readers FIRST—Mary Shelley’s "Frankenstein" or Robert Louis Stevenson’s "Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde"?
clues.ahaFactoid: Eighteen-year-old Mary Shelley drafted Frankenstein during stormy 1816 in Geneva, nearly seventy years before Jekyll’s London potion.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which epic mythological text was written FIRST—Virgil’s Roman "Aeneid" or Snorri Sturluson’s Icelandic "Prose Edda"?
clues.ahaFactoid: Virgil composed the Aeneid around 19 BCE under Emperor Augustus, over twelve hundred years before Snorri compiled Norse myths in 1220 CE.

clues.stem: Before or After? Inside Washington Irving’s "Sketch Book," which Hudson Valley legend appeared in an earlier serialized installment—Rip Van Winkle or the Headless Horseman?
clues.ahaFactoid: Irving printed Rip Van Winkle’s 20-year Catskills nap in June 1819, nine months before Ichabod Crane rode out of Sleepy Hollow.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which Arthurian verse masterpiece came FIRST—the anonymous "Sir Gawain and the Green Knight" or Edmund Spenser’s "The Faerie Queene"?
clues.ahaFactoid: A Cheshire-dialect poet spun the Green Knight’s Yuletide challenge around 1390, two centuries before Spenser praised Elizabeth I in 1590.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which British mystery phrase hit newspapers FIRST—Scottish "Loch Ness Monster" craze or Royal Air Force "gremlins" sabotaging planes?
clues.ahaFactoid: Inverness headlines launched modern Nessie mania in May 1933, while British pilots popularized mischievous gremlins during World War II.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which medieval heroic epic was written down FIRST—Iceland’s "Volsunga Saga" or the Middle High German "Nibelungenlied"?
clues.ahaFactoid: Danube-region poets composed the Nibelungenlied around 1200 CE, roughly half a century before Icelanders wrote down the Volsunga Saga.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which foundational Arthurian source appeared FIRST—Geoffrey of Monmouth’s Latin "History" or Chrétien de Troyes introducing Lancelot?
clues.ahaFactoid: Geoffrey spun Arthur’s British saga around 1136; French poet Chrétien invented Lancelot and the Holy Grail quest forty years later.
