clues.stem: Before or After? Which Ming Dynasty Chinese classic reached print earlier in the 1500s—Monkey King epic "Journey to the West" or outlaw saga "Water Margin"?
clues.ahaFactoid: Water Margin circulated in early 1500s editions well ahead of Wu Cheng’en’s definitive 1592 print edition of Journey to the West.

clues.stem: Before or After? Which surviving ancient Mediterranean romance came FIRST—Apuleius’s "Cupid and Psyche" inside The Golden Ass or Heliodorus’s "Aethiopica"?
clues.ahaFactoid: North African writer Apuleius tucked Cupid and Psyche into his second-century novel, at least a century before Heliodorus.

clues.stem: In Greek myth, one direct gaze into the eyes of snake-haired Gorgon Medusa instantly turned onlookers into what solid material?
clues.ahaFactoid: Even after Perseus beheaded Medusa using his gleaming shield as a mirror, her severed head kept its petrifying stare.

clues.stem: Why did King Arthur seat his knights around a Round Table instead of a traditional long rectangular banquet board?
clues.ahaFactoid: With zero "head of the table," every knight held equal honor—ending bloody squabbles over who sat closest to the king.

clues.stem: Which sharp household sewing-room hazard put Princess Aurora into a century-long slumber in Sleeping Beauty?
clues.ahaFactoid: Even though the king burned every spinning wheel in the realm, an old woman in a forgotten tower kept one whirling.

clues.stem: Before Irish immigrants discovered roomy American pumpkins, which tough root vegetable did families carve into spooky Halloween lanterns?
clues.ahaFactoid: Hollowed-out turnips and rutabagas with glowing embers inside looked positively eerie—far creepier than cheerful orange jack-o’-lanterns!

clues.stem: In Roman myth, Cupid carried golden arrows to spark instant love—what dull metal tipped the arrows he used to trigger instant repulsion?
clues.ahaFactoid: Ovid says Cupid shot Apollo with a golden arrow and nymph Daphne with lead—guaranteeing a famously awkward mythological chase.

clues.stem: In Norse legend, helmeted Valkyries swept over smoky battlefields with what sacred duty for fallen warriors?
clues.ahaFactoid: Old Norse "valkyrja" literally translates to "chooser of the slain," splitting honored souls between Odin’s Valhalla and Freyja’s Folkvangr.

clues.stem: After a vain Greek youth wasted away staring lovingly at his own pool reflection, what pale trumpet-shaped spring blossom sprouted beside the water?
clues.ahaFactoid: Meanwhile poor nymph Echo faded until only her repeating voice remained lingering inside mountain caves.

clues.stem: In Egypt’s Hall of Two Truths, a dead soul’s heart was weighed on bronze scales against what delicate emblem of truth?
clues.ahaFactoid: If the heart stayed lighter than the feather of cosmic order, the soul entered paradise; if heavy with guilt, monster Ammit gobbled it up.

clues.stem: How did young Irish hero Fionn mac Cumhaill accidentally absorb all the wisdom of the world while cooking the Salmon of Knowledge?
clues.ahaFactoid: Druid Finnegas had fished seven years for the hazelnut-fed salmon, only for his apprentice boy to blister his thumb turning the roast.

clues.stem: Hades agreed to let musician Orpheus lead Eurydice out of the Underworld on one strict condition—what single mistake doomed them near daylight?
clues.ahaFactoid: Only paces from the sunlit cavern mouth, Orpheus glanced over his shoulder to make sure she followed—and watched her vanish into shadow.

clues.stem: Folklore Bulletin: After bragging about good health or sunny plans, nervous speakers tap solid [ _____ ] to ward off bad luck.
clues.ahaFactoid: Whether calling friendly tree spirits or tapping church-pew oak, folks still reach fast for the nearest tabletop!

clues.stem: Superstition Desk: According to Roman-rooted lore, shattering a household looking glass brings [ _____ ] unlucky years until your reflection renews.
clues.ahaFactoid: Romans believed human health and spirit cycled completely every seven years—just toss the shards into running water to break the jinx.

clues.stem: Kitchen Omen: Spill salt across the supper table, and superstition warns you must toss a pinch over your [ _____ ] shoulder right into the devil’s eye.
clues.ahaFactoid: Left was long distrusted in Roman augury ("sinister" literally means left in Latin), making it the favorite spot for lurking spirits.

clues.stem: Storybook Weather Watch: Straw and sticks fly sky-high under the Big Bad Wolf’s huffing, yet the third brother’s [ _____ ] house stands firm.
clues.ahaFactoid: Early 1800s English chapbooks originally starred pixies or foxes before James Halliwell popularized the three crafty pigs.

clues.stem: Florence Toyshop Dispatch: Whenever Geppetto’s carved marionette tells a fib to the Blue Fairy, his [ _____ ] sprouts inches longer.
clues.ahaFactoid: In Carlo Collodi’s book, woodpeckers actually swoop in to peck Pinocchio’s overgrown snout back down to normal size.

clues.stem: Neverland Theater Flash: When Tinker Bell drinks Captain Hook’s poison, Peter Pan begs kids in the audience to [ _____ ] if they believe in fairies.
clues.ahaFactoid: Even cynical adult theatergoers at 1904’s London premiere burst into thunderous applause to save the glowing stage spotlight.

clues.stem: Yuletide Custom: Rooted in Norse Baldr lore and Druid harvest rites, hanging evergreen [ _____ ] above doorways invites holiday kisses.
clues.ahaFactoid: Ancient Scandinavians honored peace beneath its winter berries—swearing enemies even laid down weapons under a bough.

clues.stem: Athenian Harbor Flash: Forgetting to swap black mourning sails for white victory canvas, returning hero [ _____ ] breaks King Aegeus’s heart.
clues.ahaFactoid: Believing his son dead in Crete, King Aegeus leaped from coastal cliffs—giving the Aegean Sea its timeless name.

clues.stem: Phrygia Treasury Bulletin: Dionysus grants [ _____ ]’s greedy wish—until bread turns to hard bullion and even his beloved daughter freezes to metal.
clues.ahaFactoid: Real Phrygian king Midas ruled around 700 BCE, famous for dazzling brass treasures unearthed in Gordium’s royal tombs.

clues.stem: Syracuse Palace Note: Dionysius teaches flatterer [ _____ ] about royal anxiety by hanging a razor-sharp blade over dinner by a single strand.
clues.ahaFactoid: One glance upward at the glittering steel above his crown cured the courtier of wanting royal power in seconds flat.

clues.stem: Picture This Ancient Emblem: Coiled green vipers hiss where curls of hair belong on a terrifying face—whose mythic gaze did Greek soldiers paint on shields?
clues.ahaFactoid: Called a "Gorgoneion," her terrifying face served as a protective charm—later adopted as Gianni Versace’s famous fashion logo.

clues.stem: Picture This Museum Gallery: A pure white horse-like beast with a spiraled ivory horn rests peacefully inside a wooden fence ringed by wildflowers—name this legendary creature.
clues.ahaFactoid: Medieval apothecaries actually sold ground narwhal tusks at astronomical prices as fake "alicorn" unicorn-horn medicine.

clues.stem: Picture This Storybook Forest: Deep in birch woods, a creaky log cabin stands balanced atop two giant scaly yellow chicken legs—who brews potions inside?
clues.ahaFactoid: Rather than riding a broomstick, Baba Yaga flies across treetops inside a giant wooden mortar steering with a pestle.

clues.stem: Picture This Mosaic Tile: Rising out of foaming turquoise surf in a seashell chariot pulled by hippocamp sea-horses, a bearded god hefts a three-pronged spear—who is he?
clues.ahaFactoid: Besides storms and tidal waves, Greeks also prayed to Poseidon as "Earth-Shaker" whenever earthquakes rattled coastal cities.

clues.stem: Picture This Bazaar Stall: Concentric rings of cobalt blue, white, and black glass form a striking protective eye—what is this Mediterranean charm called?
clues.ahaFactoid: Hung over cribs, doorways, and Turkish airliners alike, the glassy gaze is believed to bounce envious stares harmlessly away.

clues.stem: Picture This Japanese Festival: Crimson-faced with a remarkably long protruding nose, black wings, and tiny monk pillbox cap—what mountain yokai is this mask?
clues.ahaFactoid: Originally pictured as bird-beaked demons, Tengu evolved into proud mountain martial-arts masters carrying feathered uchiwa fans.

clues.stem: Picture This Totem Crest: Wide carved wings crown Pacific Northwest cedar poles, rattling storm clouds whenever it blinks—name this mighty sky spirit.
clues.ahaFactoid: Across Indigenous traditions from the Pacific coast to the Great Plains, lightning flashes from the Thunderbird’s eyes.

clues.stem: Picture This Greek Vase: Limping beside blazing bellows with tongs and hammer in hand, which Olympian smith forged Achilles’ shield and Zeus’s bolts?
clues.ahaFactoid: Working beneath volcanic Mount Etna with Cyclops helpers, he crafted golden mechanical maidens centuries before modern robotics.

clues.stem: Picture This Temple Carving: Smiling beneath a royal crown with an elephant head, four arms, and a single whole tusk while clutching a sweet dumpling—who removes obstacles?
clues.ahaFactoid: Hindu legend says Ganesha snapped off his own right tusk to use as a fast stylus when dictating the epic Mahabharata!

clues.stem: Picture This Finnish Canvas: Brave sea-raiders fight off giant winged hag Louhi atop a wooden longship over a gleaming mill that grinds flour, salt, and gold—name that artifact.
clues.ahaFactoid: Akseli Gallen-Kallela’s 1896 masterpiece painted the Kalevala’s final sea battle where the magic Sampo shattered into the waves.

clues.stem: Spot the Myth! Three Santa Claus origin facts are true—which viral pop-culture claim about his bright red suit is commercial folklore?
clues.ahaFactoid: Cartoonists, greeting cards, and Puck covers dressed Santa in crimson decades before Haddon Sundblom’s cozy 1931 Coca-Cola paintings.

clues.stem: Spot the Myth! Three nursery rhyme histories hold up—which grim claim about "Ring Around the Rosie" lacks any 17th-century evidence?
clues.ahaFactoid: Folklorists point out the rhyme never surfaced in print until 1881—over two centuries after London’s 1665 plague—with joyful variants.

clues.stem: Spot the Myth! Three Groundhog Day facts are accurate—which boast about Punxsutawney Phil’s winter forecasts fails the weather check?
clues.ahaFactoid: NOAA climatologists checked decades of Phil’s shadow calls and found his accuracy hovers right around a coin flip—under 40 percent!

clues.stem: Spot the Myth! Three cat-folklore facts are true—which popular superstition claim gets reversed across different countries?
clues.ahaFactoid: In Britain, Scotland, and Japan, crossing paths with a black cat or welcoming one onto a fishing boat is hailed as sparkling good luck!

clues.stem: Spot the Myth! Three Snow White facts check out—which detail about the Seven Dwarfs actually came from Walt Disney, not the Brothers Grimm?
clues.ahaFactoid: In the 1812 Brothers Grimm tale, the seven little miners were completely nameless—Disney’s 1937 writers invented Doc, Dopey, and Grumpy!

clues.stem: Spot the Myth! Three facts about unicorn lore check out—which medieval belief about catching wild unicorns was never part of real natural history?
clues.ahaFactoid: Medieval nobles bought arctic whale ivory and wove hunting scenes of maidens, yet zero winged fossil skeletons ever existed.

clues.stem: Spot the Myth! Three Friday the 13th trivia facts are solid—which neat origin story connecting it to the 1307 Knights Templar arrest is modern invention?
clues.ahaFactoid: Historians note zero medieval records call Friday the 13th unlucky—the superstition largely fused in the late 1800s and a 1907 novel!

clues.stem: Spot the Myth! Three fairy-tale origin facts are solid—which assumption about classic Grimm editions shocks folks who read the 1812 originals?
clues.ahaFactoid: Early 1812 Grimm printings featured brutal villains, wicked biological mothers, and red-hot iron dancing shoes before Wilhelm softened them for kids.

clues.stem: Spot the Myth! Three Norse mythology facts check out—which fiery modern picture of Helheim contradicts Snorri’s icy Eddas?
clues.ahaFactoid: Far from roaring lava flames, Norse Helheim (Niflhel) was freezing, misty, and bleak—where ordinary folk who didn’t die in battle rested.

clues.stem: Spot the Myth! Three classical Greek myth facts check out—which popular assumption about early Homeric Greeks and the sun chariot is slightly off?
clues.ahaFactoid: In early Greece, Titan Helios drove the blazing sun across the sky while Apollo stayed music-and-light—later Roman poets merged their jobs!

clues.stem: Mythic Creature Split: In traditional Scottish and medieval folklore, does a classic unicorn sprout feathered wings or just a single spiral horn?
clues.ahaFactoid: Pop culture sometimes mashes winged Pegasus and the unicorn into an "alicorn," yet traditional unicorns stayed firmly earthbound.

clues.stem: Homecoming Check: After twenty years away from Ithaca, who recognized disguised beggar Odysseus right away—old hound Argos or suitors at the feast?
clues.ahaFactoid: Lying weak on a courtyard dung heap, loyal Argos wagged his tail and dropped his ears one final time upon hearing his master’s voice.

clues.stem: Fairy-Tale Split: How long did Sleeping Beauty sleep inside her thorny castle tower before the spell broke—a full century nap or just ten winters?
clues.ahaFactoid: The good fairy softened the death curse into an unbroken hundred-year slumber so the whole palace slept peacefully alongside the princess.

clues.stem: Camelot Check: In Malory’s Le Morte d’Arthur, how did young Arthur prove his royal right as king—pulling a blade from stone or fishing it from a pond?

clues.stem: Monster Check: In classical Greek mythology, what writhed atop Medusa’s head—living venomous snakes or flickering flames?

clues.stem: Celtic Calendar: Did ancient Irish Samhain—ancestral root of Halloween—mark the joyful start of spring or the end of summer harvest?

clues.stem: Asgard Workshop: Giant wolf Fenrir snapped thick iron chains effortlessly—what held him fast in the end, dwarf-spun silk ribbon or dragon-scale steel?
clues.ahaFactoid: Gleipnir was forged from six impossible things: a cat’s footsteps, a woman’s beard, mountain roots, bear sinews, fish breath, and bird spit.

clues.stem: Shinto Shrine Check: Outside Japanese Inari rice shrines, sleek fox statues guard the gates holding keys or scrolls—what do "Kitsune" foxes represent here?

clues.stem: Mesopotamian Tablet: Searching for eternal life after Enkidu’s death, who told Gilgamesh the secret story of surviving the Great Flood—Utnapishtim or Hammurabi?

clues.stem: Mid-Autumn Lore: After swallowing the Queen Mother of the West’s immortality elixir, which heavenly orb did Chang’e float up to live upon—the Moon or Venus?
clues.ahaFactoid: Her husband archer Hou Yi honored her every autumn night with round cakes and fruit—inspiring today’s joyful Mid-Autumn mooncake festival.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Rolling two fair six-sided dice, which total comes up MORE often—lucky seven or boxcars twelve?
clues.ahaFactoid: Six different combinations sum to 7 (one in six rolls), whereas only 6+6 makes 12—making 7 six times more likely.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Surprise anatomy check: which mammal packs MORE individual bones inside its neck—a towering giraffe or a tiny house mouse?
clues.ahaFactoid: Almost every mammal—humans, giraffes, whales, and mice—has seven neck vertebrae; giraffes simply grow enormous foot-long bones!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Which blazes HOTTER in temperature—a bolt of Earth lightning or the visible surface of the Sun?
clues.ahaFactoid: Lightning superheats surrounding air to roughly 50,000 degrees Fahrenheit—nearly five times hotter than the Sun’s 10,000-degree photosphere!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Compared to the old "blind as a bat" proverb, how sharp is a typical fruit bat’s actual vision compared to total blindness?
clues.ahaFactoid: No bat species is blind! Microbats see finely alongside echolocation, and big flying foxes often spot ripe fruit better than humans at dusk.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Weight-for-weight myth check: which drops FASTER inside a vacuum chamber with zero air resistance—a bowling ball or a feather?
clues.ahaFactoid: Apollo 15’s Dave Scott proved Galileo right live on the Moon in 1971, dropping a falcon feather and hammer that landed together.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? At a fair American roulette wheel after ten Reds in a row, how do the odds of Black on spin eleven compare to Red?
clues.ahaFactoid: Casino wheels have zero memory! Calling Black "overdue" is the classic Gambler’s Fallacy—both Red and Black remain 18 in 38.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Where does plain water start boiling at a LOWER thermometer temperature—at sea level or atop Mount Everest?
clues.ahaFactoid: Thin mountain air presses down far less on the pot, letting water boil around 154 degrees Fahrenheit on Everest—too cool for decent pasta!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? How much true white pigment lives inside a polar bear’s hollow hair shafts compared to jet-black melanin under its skin?
clues.ahaFactoid: Polar bear hairs are actually clear, hollow tubes that scatter visible light white over pitch-black heat-absorbing skin!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Contrary to the "half your heat escapes through your head" myth, what share does an uncovered head actually lose in cold air?
clues.ahaFactoid: Your head holds under ten percent of body surface area; the old army test only felt huge because soldiers wore arctic parkas without hats!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? On neighboring planet Venus, which stretches LONGER in Earth days—one slow spin on its axis or one orbit around the Sun?
clues.ahaFactoid: Venus spins backward so sluggishly that a full sidereal rotation takes 243 Earth days—longer than its 225-day trip around the Sun!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Which gap of years is LONGER—Cleopatra back to the Great Pyramid’s construction, or Cleopatra forward to the first iPhone?
clues.ahaFactoid: Egypt built Giza’s Great Pyramid around 2560 BCE, roughly 2,500 years before Cleopatra—whereas only ~2,037 years separate her from 2007!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Which famous institution lasted or started EARLIER—teaching at Oxford University or the founding of the Aztec Empire?
clues.ahaFactoid: Scholars taught at Oxford by 1096 CE—more than three centuries before the Aztec Triple Alliance formed Tenochtitlan in 1428!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Deep-time surprise: which lineage swam or sprouted on Earth for MORE millions of years—ocean sharks or woody trees?
clues.ahaFactoid: Fossil shark scales date back over 400 million years, predating the earliest true trees by tens of millions of years—and even Saturn’s rings!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Brain-bending scale check: how long does one BILLION seconds take compared to one MILLION seconds’ eleven and a half days?
clues.ahaFactoid: Human intuition stumbles badly on big zeros: a million seconds is under two weeks, while a billion seconds spans roughly 31.7 years!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Which sweater fiber keeps MORE insulating warmth when soaked in cold rain—sheep’s wool or plain cotton?
clues.ahaFactoid: Cotton collapses when wet and conducts heat away fast ("cotton kills"), whereas crimped wool fibers trap air pockets and even warm slightly as they absorb mist.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Which time gap is BIGGER—between Stegosaurus and Tyrannosaurus rex, or between Tyrannosaurus rex and modern humans?
clues.ahaFactoid: Roughly 85 million years separated Jurassic Stegosaurus from Cretaceous T-Rex—while only 66 million years separate T-Rex from us!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? In Kahneman’s cab puzzle, 85% of city cabs are Green and 15% Blue; if an 80%-accurate witness spots a Blue cab, which is MORE likely guilty?
clues.ahaFactoid: Base-rate neglect fools us! Out of 100 cabs, 12 true Blue hits compete against 17 false-alarm Green cabs—meaning Green still tops 58%!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? If you could fold a standard 0.1 mm sheet of paper neatly in half 42 times, how would its stack compare to the distance to the Moon?
clues.ahaFactoid: Exponential doubling turns 0.1 mm times two-to-the-42nd into 439,800 kilometers—comfortably passing the 384,400 km Moon!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Classic puzzle twist: compared to knowing "at least one of two kids is a boy" (1/3 odds of two boys), does "born on Tuesday" raise or lower the odds?
clues.ahaFactoid: Adding the rare weekday qualifier shrinks the two-girl/mixed pool faster than the two-boy overlap, shifting odds from 33% up to 48.1%!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Under Zipf’s linguistic law in large books, how often does the #1 word ("the") appear compared to #2 ("of")?
clues.ahaFactoid: Across novels and Wikipedia alike, rank-n word frequency drops smoothly near 1/n—making #1 appear roughly twice as often as #2.

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? In David Hilbert’s Grand Hotel paradox, if all infinite rooms are FULL, how many new guests can still fit by shifting everyone one room up?
clues.ahaFactoid: Moving every guest from room n to room 2n frees every odd room—proving countable infinity swallows another countable infinity whole!

clues.stem: Higher or Lower? Under Lewis Fry Richardson’s Coastline Paradox, how does Britain’s measured shoreline change as you switch to a SMALLER ruler?
clues.ahaFactoid: Smaller rulers hug tinier coves, pebbles, and fractals—causing measured length to climb without any finite limit!

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Classic calendar trick: three of these months have 31 days—which shorter month stops neatly at 30?
clues.ahaFactoid: The old knuckle-bump rhyme never lies: thirty days hath September, April, June, and November!

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these creepy-crawlies are true six-legged insects—which eight-legged arachnid crashes the bug lineup?
clues.ahaFactoid: Spiders, scorpions, and ticks pack eight legs and two body segments, unlike six-legged insects.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Botanically speaking, three of these salad staples are true seed-bearing fruits—which crunchy orange root actually comes from underground?
clues.ahaFactoid: Tomatoes, cucumbers, and bell peppers grow from blossoms and hold seeds inside, whereas carrots are pure taproots!

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these pantry picks are actually culinary seeds or drupes, NOT true botanical nuts—which autumn tree seed IS a real botanical nut?
clues.ahaFactoid: Peanuts are underground legumes while almonds and cashews are drupe seeds—only hard-shelled chestnuts, hazelnuts, and acorns count as true nuts!

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these animals are true ocean-dwelling mammals—which tuxedoed swimmer lays eggs as a bird?
clues.ahaFactoid: Whales, dolphins, and manatees nurse live young with milk; penguins dive deep too, yet hatch from Antarctic eggs.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these popular schoolbook "facts" are completely false myths—which quirky detail actually checks out as true?
clues.ahaFactoid: Washington really did wear uncomfortable dentures of hippo ivory, brass, and human teeth—not wood, as myth claims!

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these names sound like animals yet are actually plants or minerals—which one is a genuine living animal?
clues.ahaFactoid: Though anchored quietly to seafloors like coral, sea sponges are multi-celled aquatic animals that pump water through tiny pores!

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Botanical plot twist: three of these foods count as true scientific berries—which red fruit with outside seeds is NOT a true berry?
clues.ahaFactoid: Bananas, kiwis, and eggplants sprout from a single flower ovary with inner seeds—while strawberries grow seeds on their outside!

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these everyday body myths are completely bogus—which body fact is genuinely true?
clues.ahaFactoid: Shaving only leaves a blunt tip that feels stubbly, whereas tongue maps, head-burying ostriches, and warty toads are pure fiction!

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these calendar months still carry Latin number roots (7, 8, 10)—which month was renamed for dictator Julius Caesar?
clues.ahaFactoid: Originally "Quintilis" (fifth), July honored Julius Caesar—and pushed Sept-, Oct-, Nov-, Dec- two slots out of sync later!

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these movie catchphrases were slightly misremembered by fans—which famous line was actually spoken word-for-word on screen?
clues.ahaFactoid: Bogart really said "Here’s looking at you, kid" in Casablanca, whereas the other three iconic lines never appeared in those exact words!

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these terms describe real psychological biases—which name belongs to an impossible triangle drawing instead?
clues.ahaFactoid: Lionel and Roger Penrose sketched the impossible looping tribar in 1958, inspiring M.C. Escher’s mind-bending prints.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these creatures are misnamed (a marsupial, a rodent, a fish)—which creature actually belongs to its stated animal family?
clues.ahaFactoid: Koalas aren’t bears, guinea pigs aren’t pigs, and flying foxes are giant bats—only the fearless honey badger is a true mustelid badger cousin!

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these tricks fool your eyes on static paper—which auditory trick uses two mismatched headphone tones to pulse in your ears?
clues.ahaFactoid: Play 300 Hz in one ear and 310 Hz in the other, and your brainstem invents a phantom 10-Hz rhythmic pulse out of thin air.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these logic traps attack the person, twist their words, or dodge the issue—which one is a valid deductive proof rule?

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these puzzles come from strategic game theory—which ancient Greek paradox asks how many removed grains still leave a sand heap?
clues.ahaFactoid: Philosopher Eubulides asked when a heap stops being a heap one grain at a time—exposing the fuzziness of everyday language.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these terms describe collective or personal memory glitches—which term names a visual illusion of motion on flickering LED lights?
clues.ahaFactoid: Max Wertheimer named the phi phenomenon in 1912 when rapid flashing bulbs fooled eyes into seeing smooth movement.

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these Latin phrases name classic reasoning fallacies—which courtroom Latin phrase simply means "friend of the court"?
clues.ahaFactoid: Outside experts file amicus curiae briefs to inform judges—not to pull sneaky circular arguments or false-cause tricks!

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these biases explain irrational consumer pricing quirks—which fallacy claims smashing shop glass boosts total prosperity?

clues.stem: Odd One Out! Three of these terms name sneaky data biases—which theorem guarantees sample averages converge toward the true mean as samples grow?
clues.ahaFactoid: Bernoulli’s Law of Large Numbers is probability’s bedrock anchor, unlike Berkson’s hospital-collision bias or ecological confusion.

clues.stem: Finish the famous digital-age satire line jokingly pinned on Abraham Lincoln: "Don’t believe everything you read on the [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Lincoln died 104 years before ARPANET sent its first packet—making this joke quote the ultimate poster child for fake citations!

clues.stem: Finish the classic warning against get-rich-quick scams: "A fool and his money are soon [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: English poet Thomas Tusser coined a rhyming version back in 1557—proving scammers and gullible buyers are timeless!

clues.stem: Finish the everyday idiom mocking folks who brag after the results are already in: "Hindsight is [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Psychologists call it "knew-it-all-along" bias—once an outcome occurs, our brains rewrite past uncertainty into inevitability.

clues.stem: Finish the carpenter’s golden rule against hasty blunders: "Measure twice, cut [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Russian and English folk proverbs alike preached measuring seven times before a single slice—cheaper than wasting good oak!

clues.stem: Finish the classic comparison trap proverb: "The grass is always greener on the other [ _____ ]."

clues.stem: Finish the Aesop fable moral warning the fox and goat alike: "Look before you [ _____ ]."

clues.stem: Finish the classic proverb about learning caution from a painful mistake: "Once bitten, twice [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Similar sayings appear across cultures, from Chinese "bitten by a snake, scared of a rope" to English "burnt child dreads the fire."

clues.stem: Finish the ancient proverb warning against hubris and overconfidence: "Pride goes before a [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Adapted from the Book of Proverbs, the warning reminds winners that overconfidence turns small cracks into collapses.

clues.stem: Finish the blunt Scottish-rooted reality check on wishful thinking: "If wishes were horses, beggars would [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: First recorded in James Carmichael’s 1628 Scots proverb collection, it’s still the fastest way to burst daydream budgets.

clues.stem: Finish the German-origin warning against discarding good ideas alongside minor flaws: "Don’t throw the baby out with the [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Thomas Murner coined the vivid image in 1512; philosopher Thomas Carlyle brought it into everyday English in 1849.

clues.stem: Finish the plainspoken abductive-reasoning test often traced to James Whitcomb Riley: "If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it’s a [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: The "duck test" works wonderfully for quick pattern matching, until a clever decoy shows up wearing convincing feathers!

clues.stem: Finish René Descartes’s famous bedrock antidote to radical doubt ("Cogito, ergo sum"): "I think, therefore I [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Even if an evil demon deceived every sense, Descartes argued, doubting itself proved a thinking mind existed.

clues.stem: Finish aerospace engineer Edward Murphy Jr.’s famous 1949 warning about reversed sensor plugs: "Whatever can go [ _____ ], will."
clues.ahaFactoid: Col. John Stapp popularized Murphy’s Law at a press conference after rocket-sled decelerators recorded zero data because every gauge was wired backward.

clues.stem: Finish C. Northcote Parkinson’s satirical 1955 Economist essay maxim: "Work expands so as to fill the [ _____ ] available for its completion."
clues.ahaFactoid: Parkinson watched British Admiralty bureaucracy swell even as the Royal Navy shrank, proving meetings multiply to match open calendars.

clues.stem: Finish Laurence J. Peter’s sharp 1969 satire of corporate promotions: "In a hierarchy, every employee tends to rise to his level of [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Because good workers keep getting promoted until they hit a job they’re bad at, Peter joked, every desk eventually stalls!

clues.stem: Finish sci-fi writer Theodore Sturgeon’s witty defense when critics trashed science fiction: "Ninety percent of [ _____ ] is crud."
clues.ahaFactoid: Sturgeon argued judging a whole genre by its worst pulp ignores that 90 percent of mysteries, poems, and movies are mediocre too.

clues.stem: Finish Alberto Brandolini’s 2013 Misinformation Asymmetry Principle: "The amount of energy needed to refute nonsense is an order of [ _____ ] larger than to produce it."
clues.ahaFactoid: Italian programmer Brandolini tweeted the law after watching political TV debates—capturing why snappy fibs outrun careful fact-checks.

clues.stem: Finish G.K. Chesterton’s rule against tearing down old rules blindly: "Before you take down a [ _____ ], know why it was put up."
clues.ahaFactoid: Known as Chesterton’s Fence, the principle urges reformers to understand hidden guardrails before deleting weird legacy code or laws.

clues.stem: Finish philosopher George Santayana’s classic 1905 warning about history’s blunders: "Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to [ _____ ] it."
clues.ahaFactoid: Winston Churchill famously paraphrased Santayana in a 1948 House of Commons speech, cementing the line worldwide.

clues.stem: Finish baseball legend Yogi Berra’s famously contradictory restaurant complaint: "Nobody goes there anymore; it’s too [ _____ ]."
clues.ahaFactoid: Philosophers actually study "Yogi-isms" as comic self-contradictions that still somehow make total sense about peak rush-hour hotspots!

clues.stem: Finish Bertrand Russell’s classic burden-of-proof thought experiment: nobody can disprove a tiny china [ _____ ] orbiting between Earth and Mars.
clues.ahaFactoid: Russell’s Teapot shows why extraordinary claims must bring proof rather than daring skeptics to prove a negative.

clues.stem: Finish Nassim Taleb’s parable of induction failure: a fed bird feels safest on Day 1,000—right before [ _____ ] arrives.
clues.ahaFactoid: Inspired by Bertrand Russell’s inductivist chicken, the Turkey Problem warns against mistaking calm history for zero future tail risk.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? I carry 88 black and white keys across my smiling front, yet I can’t unlock a single front door—what musical furniture am I?
clues.ahaFactoid: Bartolomeo Cristofori invented my touch-sensitive hammer keyboard around 1700, naming me "gravicembalo col piano e forte."

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? I have a round face and two tireless hands spinning all day long, yet I own zero arms or legs—what ticks on your wall?
clues.ahaFactoid: Early mechanical tower clocks in medieval Europe originally lacked minute hands altogether—only striking bells on the hour!

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Sleek and silvery with one tiny oval eye near my blunt end, I pull colorful thread through cloth yet remain completely blind.
clues.ahaFactoid: Archaeologists have dug up bone sewing needles with drilled eyes dating back more than 40,000 years!

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? I have a stiff spine and hundreds of crisp leaves packed tightly together, yet I’m no tree or living creature—what sits on your nightstand?
clues.ahaFactoid: Before paper pages existed, ancient Romans wrote on bound wooden tablets coated in wax called a "codex"—Latin for tree trunk!

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Lined up with dozens of straight parallel teeth, I tidy unruly tangles every morning yet never take a single bite of breakfast.
clues.ahaFactoid: Roman and Viking travelers treasured carved ivory and antler combs enough to bury them inside royal graves.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? I travel across oceans to Paris and Tokyo while staying glued quietly in the exact same upper-right paper corner.
clues.ahaFactoid: Britain’s 1840 Penny Black introduced adhesive prepaid stamps—revolutionizing mail so receivers no longer paid at the door.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? I run tirelessly without legs, rest on a winding bed yet never sleep, and open a wide mouth into the sea.
clues.ahaFactoid: From the Nile’s fan-shaped delta to the Amazon’s colossal mouth, rivers shaped nearly every early civilization on Earth.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Fragile as glass in a crowded room—the very instant you speak my name aloud, you shatter me completely.
clues.ahaFactoid: Even an ultra-quiet library hovers near 30 decibels; an anechoic chamber gets so quiet you start hearing your own heartbeat.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Flip me for coin-toss decisions and you’ll see my shiny head and tail, though I have zero torso or legs in between.
clues.ahaFactoid: Ancient Romans actually played coin tosses calling "heads or ships" (capita aut navim) after the prow stamped on bronze asses!

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Unlike a leaky bucket, I’m riddled with hundreds of holes from top to bottom—yet somehow I still hold water cheerfully!
clues.ahaFactoid: Capillary action pulls liquid deep into microscopic cellulose and polyurethane pores until your hand squeezes it back out.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Classic brainteaser: two US coins add up to 30 cents, and ONE of them is NOT a nickel—what coin MUST the other one be?
clues.ahaFactoid: The sneaky phrasing only said ONE isn’t a nickel—the other coin IS a nickel paired with a shiny 25-cent quarter!

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? In the classic logic riddle where a father and son crash and the surgeon cries "I can’t operate, he’s my son!"—who holds the scalpel?
clues.ahaFactoid: Psychologists still use this 1970s riddle to show how automatic gender stereotypes blind readers to the obvious answer: Mom is the surgeon!

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? The dark twin of uplifting coaching—when supervisors expect someone to fail, chilly feedback and meager trust actually drag performance down!
clues.ahaFactoid: Coined by psychologist Elisha Babad in 1982 after Jewish clay-giant folklore, low expectations quietly become self-fulfilling prophecies.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Psychologist Bertram Forer handed students identical astrology blurbs ("You crave approval yet criticize yourself") and got 4.3/5 accuracy scores!

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Buy a mint-green Mini Cooper or learn a weird new word, and suddenly you spot it on every block—what cognitive trick makes it feel newly everywhere?
clues.ahaFactoid: Also nicknamed the Baader-Meinhof phenomenon, selective attention plus confirmation bias spotlights things your brain just flagged.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Researcher Robert Rosenthal told teachers random kids were hidden geniuses—and those students genuinely soared on later IQ tests through higher expectations!
clues.ahaFactoid: Named after the Greek sculptor whose belief brought stone to life, warm teacher encouragement can literally lift real classroom results.

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? One 1975 economist showed drivers protected by shiny seatbelts and airbags sometimes drive faster—partially eating up safety gains with extra risk!

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Stare steadily at a central dot inside a ring of blurry lilac blobs for 20 seconds, and watch the pastel circles vanish completely off the page!

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? A 1920s Soviet filmmaker spliced the exact same blank actor face beside soup, a coffin, and a child—fooling viewers into seeing hunger, grief, and joy!

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Proved by Darley and Latané in smoke-filled test rooms, the MORE witnesses see someone in trouble, the LESS likely any single stranger steps up to help!

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? In WWII, generals wanted to armor bullet-riddled bomber wings until a Hungarian statistician pointed at the pristine engines of returning planes—where did armor go?

clues.stem: Who or What Am I? Offered two urns—one 50/50 red-black and one mystery mix—investors overwhelmingly dodge the unknown urn even when symmetry guarantees equal odds!
clues.ahaFactoid: Pentagon Papers whistleblower Daniel Ellsberg first published this famous ambiguity-aversion economics puzzle in 1961!

clues.stem: Before or After? Which myth-shattering TV favorite aired its very first episode FIRST—Discovery’s "MythBusters" or BBC’s "QI"?
clues.ahaFactoid: MythBusters tested JATO rocket cars in January 2003—just months before Stephen Fry rang the first Klaxon on QI in September 2003!
